domain.title: Distributed Systems
domain.tag: consensus · consistency · time · failure · the papers
domain.why: This is what happens when a program isn't running on one computer anymore, but many, all talking to each other, any of which can fail or lie about the time. It's the part of computer science where confident-sounding wrong answers are most common, because the failure cases are hard to picture. Getting the actual definitions right instead of the folk versions everyone repeats is one of the clearest signs that you really understand a system.

sections.note: the assumptions every proof in this domain quantifies over

L0.body:
Timing models, as assumptions about message delay $\delta$ and relative process speed:

  synchronous           a bound $\Delta$ on $\delta$ exists, is known, and always holds
  partially synchronous  a bound $\Delta$ exists but is unknown; or is known
                         but only holds after some unknown Global Stabilisation Time
  asynchronous          no bound on $\delta$ exists at all

Consensus with $f < n/2$ crash faults: solvable in the first two, impossible in the third.
L0.cloze:
synchronous           a bound on delay exists, is {{c1::known}}, and always holds
  partially synchronous  a bound exists but is {{c2::unknown}}, or holds only after {{c3::GST}}
  asynchronous          {{c4::no bound}} on delay exists

Consensus with $f < n/2$ crash faults is impossible in the {{c5::asynchronous}} model.

concepts.L1: Three assumptions about timing, not three kinds of network. Synchronous: a known bound on message delay and process speed. Asynchronous: no bound exists. Partially synchronous: a bound exists but you do not know it, or it only holds eventually.
concepts.L2: The model is a proof device, not a description of your network. Assuming asynchrony does not make a system more robust; it makes termination unprovable. Every consensus protocol you will ship, Raft included, is a partial-synchrony algorithm wearing a timeout.
concepts.L3: The reason the middle model exists is that the two extremes are both useless. Under full synchrony you can detect a crash perfectly: wait $\Delta$, and silence means death. That model does not survive a GC pause. Under full asynchrony you can never distinguish a crashed process from a slow one, which is precisely the lever FLP pulls. Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer's 1988 partial synchrony model says: assume the bound holds eventually, from some unknown time $T$ onward. Safety is then proved for all executions including the bad prefix, while liveness is only promised after $T$. That split, safety always and liveness eventually, is the shape of every practical protocol in this domain.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team argues their service 'assumes an asynchronous network, so it is safe under any timing'. They then add a {ms} ms leader-election timeout. State precisely which model their system is now in, and which of safety and liveness that timeout is buying.
L4.answer: Partial synchrony. The timeout does not buy safety; safety must hold in all executions including ones where the timeout fires wrongly. It buys liveness: it guarantees a stalled leader is eventually replaced, so the protocol makes progress once the network behaves.
L4.explanation: The common error is thinking a timeout makes the system synchronous, or that it protects correctness. A timeout is a liveness device. If a false timeout can break your invariants, the protocol was already unsafe.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the asynchronous model, why can no algorithm distinguish a process that has crashed from one that is merely slow? Answer in one sentence, then say what that implies for a {kind} failure detector.
L4.answer: Because no bound on message delay exists, any silence of finite length is consistent with both a crash and an arbitrarily slow-but-alive process, so no finite observation separates them. A perfect detector (no false suspicions, ever) is therefore unimplementable; only eventually-accurate detectors are.
L4.explanation: This indistinguishability is the whole content of the asynchronous model and the engine of the FLP proof. Every practical detector accepts false positives in exchange for bounded detection time.

L0.body:
The fault-model ladder, weakest to strongest adversary:

  crash-stop      a process halts and never returns
  crash-recovery  a process halts, then restarts with only its stable storage
  omission        a process drops some sends or receives but is otherwise correct
  Byzantine       a process may do anything, including lie differently to different peers

Tolerating $f$ faults needs $n \geq 2f+1$ for the first three, $n \geq 3f+1$ for Byzantine.

concepts.L1: A ladder of adversaries, each strictly containing the one below. What changes as you climb is not the algorithm's shape but its cost: the number of replicas, the number of message rounds, and whether you need cryptography.
concepts.L2: Crash-recovery, not crash-stop, is the model your code actually lives in, and it is the one people skip. A recovered node has amnesia about everything it did not fsync, so any protocol variable you keep only in memory is a correctness bug the moment a machine reboots.
concepts.L3: The jump from $2f+1$ to $3f+1$ has a clean reason. With crash faults, a quorum of $f+1$ out of $2f+1$ always intersects any other quorum in at least one node, and that node is honest because crashed nodes say nothing. With Byzantine faults the intersection may contain a liar, so you need the intersection to have at least $f+1$ nodes, of which at most $f$ lie, leaving one honest witness. Quorums of size $q$ from $n$ intersect in $2q - n$ nodes; requiring $2q - n \geq f+1$ with $q = n - f$ gives $n \geq 3f+1$. Crash-recovery sits between: no lying, but a node can forget, which is why Raft demands currentTerm and votedFor be on disk before any reply.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must tolerate $f = {f}$ faults. Give the minimum cluster size and the quorum size for (a) the crash-fault model and (b) the Byzantine model. Answer with the minimum Byzantine cluster size.
L4.answer: Crash: $n = 2f+1$, quorum $f+1$. Byzantine: $n = 3f+1$, quorum $2f+1$. For $f=1$: 3 and 2, versus 4 and 3. For $f=2$: 5 and 3, versus 7 and 5. For $f=3$: 7 and 4, versus 10 and 7. For $f=4$: 9 and 5, versus 13 and 9.
L4.explanation: The Byzantine quorum $2f+1$ out of $3f+1$ is chosen so any two quorums share at least $f+1$ nodes, guaranteeing one honest node in common. Check: $2(2f+1) - (3f+1) = f+1$.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Raft implementation keeps currentTerm in memory and writes it to disk asynchronously every {t} ms for throughput. Describe a crash-recovery execution in which two leaders are elected in the same term.
L4.answer: Node A votes for X in term 7, replies, then crashes before the flush. On restart it reads a stale term (say 5) and has no record of the vote. Candidate Y now requests votes for term 7; A sees 7 as new, votes again. X and Y each collect a majority in term 7 and both become leader, so two logs can be committed at the same index.
L4.explanation: This is the concrete cost of ignoring crash-recovery. Raft's persistence rule is not an optimisation detail: currentTerm, votedFor and the log must be durable before any RPC reply, or the one-vote-per-term invariant is unenforceable.

L0.body:
Alpern and Schneider's decomposition. Every property is an intersection of one of each.

  safety    "nothing bad ever happens"    violated by a FINITE prefix
  liveness  "something good eventually"    violated only by an INFINITE trace

Consensus splits into:
  agreement, validity   (safety)  -- must hold in every execution
  termination           (liveness) -- what FLP proves you cannot guarantee
L0.cloze:
safety    violated by a {{c1::finite}} prefix
  liveness  violated only by an {{c2::infinite}} trace

Consensus: agreement and validity are {{c3::safety}}; termination is {{c4::liveness}}, and it is the one {{c5::FLP}} shows you cannot guarantee asynchronously.

concepts.L1: A partition of correctness properties by how they can be violated. A safety violation has a finite witness: a prefix of the run after which no continuation is acceptable. A liveness violation has no finite witness; you must watch forever.
concepts.L2: Almost every argument about consistency versus availability is really a safety-versus-liveness argument, and the two are traded, never both maximised. A system that returns an error is live-failing but safe; a system that returns a wrong value is available and unsafe.
concepts.L3: The test is mechanical: can you point at a moment and say 'it is already broken'? Two leaders in one term, a read that returns a value never written, a committed entry that later disappears: all finite, all safety. 'The cluster eventually elects a leader' has no such moment, since at any instant it might elect one next. This is why FLP is survivable. FLP forbids guaranteed termination, a liveness property; it says nothing about agreement. So real protocols make safety unconditional and liveness conditional on timing. It is also why model checkers treat the two differently: safety is a reachability check, liveness needs fairness assumptions and cycle detection over the state graph.

L4.prompt_tpl: Classify each as safety or liveness, and give the finite witness where one exists: (a) 'no two clients hold the lock at once', (b) 'every request is eventually answered', (c) 'reads never return a value older than the client's own last write', (d) 'the cluster elects a leader within {s} seconds'.
L4.answer: (a) safety, witness is the instant both hold it. (b) liveness, no finite witness. (c) safety, witness is the stale read. (d) safety under a bounded model: the witness is the moment the deadline passes with no leader. A bounded liveness claim is a safety property.
L4.explanation: Item (d) is the trap. Adding a real-time bound converts a liveness property into a safety property, which is why timeouts are testable and 'eventually' is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Raft is claimed to be safe even when {n} nodes suffer arbitrary clock skew and message reordering. Explain which of Raft's five properties this claim covers and which one it deliberately excludes.
L4.answer: It covers the safety properties: election safety, leader append-only, log matching, leader completeness, state-machine safety. It excludes liveness. Skew and reordering can prevent a leader ever being elected; randomised timeouts make that unlikely but do not make it impossible, which is exactly the FLP-permitted gap.
L4.explanation: Ongaro and Ousterhout prove the five safety properties unconditionally and discuss liveness separately under a timing assumption. Any protocol claiming both unconditionally is either assuming synchrony or is wrong.

L0.body:
Lamport's relation $\rightarrow$ on events, the smallest relation satisfying:

  1. if $a$ and $b$ are in the same process and $a$ precedes $b$, then $a \to b$
  2. if $a$ is the send of a message and $b$ its receive, then $a \to b$
  3. transitivity: $a \to b$ and $b \to c$ imply $a \to c$

$a$ and $b$ are concurrent, written $a \parallel b$, iff neither $a \to b$ nor $b \to a$.
This is a strict partial order, not a total order.

concepts.L1: The only ordering a distributed system can observe without clocks. Three rules, closed under transitivity. It is a partial order, so the honest answer to 'which happened first' is often 'neither, they are concurrent'.
concepts.L2: Happens-before is potential causality, not causality. If $a \to b$, then $a$ could have influenced $b$; it does not mean it did. And two events can be genuinely causally linked through a channel outside the system (a phone call, a shared user) while the relation calls them concurrent.
concepts.L3: Build the relation on a three-process trace. $P_1$ sends $m_1$ to $P_2$; $P_2$ receives it and sends $m_2$ to $P_3$. Then $\mathrm{send}(m_1) \to \mathrm{recv}(m_1) \to \mathrm{send}(m_2) \to \mathrm{recv}(m_2)$ by rules 2, 1, 2 and transitivity. Meanwhile a local event $e$ on $P_3$ before $\mathrm{recv}(m_2)$ is concurrent with everything on $P_1$: no chain of sends and program order connects them. That is why concurrency is the common case, not the exception. Every mechanism later in this domain is either a way to encode this order (Lamport timestamps, vector clocks, HLC) or a way to impose a total order on top of it (consensus).

L4.prompt_tpl: Trace: $P_1$ does $a$ then sends $m$; $P_2$ does $b$, receives $m$, then does $c$; $P_3$ does $d$ with no messages at all in this run. For the pair set given, list every pair related by happens-before and every concurrent pair, with {n} processes in play.
L4.answer: Related: $a \to \mathrm{send}(m) \to \mathrm{recv}(m) \to c$, and $b \to \mathrm{recv}(m) \to c$, plus all transitive closures. Concurrent: $a \parallel b$, $\mathrm{send}(m) \parallel b$, and $d$ is concurrent with every other event in the run since $P_3$ neither sends nor receives.
L4.explanation: The point of the exercise is $a \parallel b$: $a$ precedes $\mathrm{recv}(m)$ and $b$ precedes $\mathrm{recv}(m)$, but nothing orders $a$ against $b$. An isolated process is concurrent with everything.

L4.prompt_tpl: A user posts a comment on server A, then phones a friend who reads it on server B, {sec} seconds later, before replication completes. Does happens-before capture this ordering? What is the standard name for what leaked?
L4.answer: No. The relation only sees in-system program order and message send/receive; the phone call is an out-of-band channel. This is a hidden or external causality channel, and it is why causal consistency alone cannot prevent every user-visible anomaly, and why linearizability's real-time constraint exists.
L4.explanation: This is the practical gap between causal and linearizable. Linearizability's real-time ordering closes out-of-band channels because it orders by wall-clock instants, not by message chains.

concepts.t: Failure detector classes and the weakest one

L0.body:
Chandra and Toueg's classification, by two properties:

  completeness  every crashed process is eventually permanently suspected
  accuracy      correct processes are not (wrongly) suspected

  P    perfect             strong completeness + strong accuracy
  S    strong              strong completeness + weak accuracy
  <>P  eventually perfect  accuracy holds only after some unknown time
  <>S  eventually strong   the weakest class that still solves consensus for $f < n/2$
  Omega                    outputs one leader, eventually the same correct one everywhere

concepts.L1: An abstraction that isolates exactly how much synchrony consensus needs. A detector is an oracle each process queries for a list of suspects; the classes differ in how wrong it may be and for how long.
concepts.L2: The result is not that detectors make consensus possible; it is that Omega, 'eventually one correct leader agreed by all', is the weakest oracle that does. Every leader-based protocol, Raft included, is Omega implemented with timeouts, and its correctness never depends on the detector being right.
concepts.L3: Chandra, Hadzilacos and Toueg proved that $\Diamond S$, and equivalently $\Omega$, is the weakest failure detector solving consensus with a majority of correct processes. The proof matters practically: it tells you exactly where to put your timing assumptions. Safety must be independent of the detector, because the detector is allowed to be arbitrarily wrong for an arbitrarily long prefix. Liveness may depend on it, because eventually it stops lying. Read Raft against this: election safety comes from terms and the one-vote rule, which hold no matter how wildly timeouts misfire; progress comes from randomised timeouts eventually producing a single candidate, which is $\Omega$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your service raises the health-check timeout from {a} ms to {b} ms after a spate of false failovers. In failure-detector terms, name the property you improved, the one you degraded, and state which of safety and liveness each maps to.
L4.answer: You improved accuracy (fewer wrong suspicions) and degraded completeness in the timely sense: real crashes are now detected far later. Accuracy failures cost liveness through unnecessary elections and lost work; slow completeness costs availability, since a dead leader is tolerated longer. Neither should affect safety.
L4.explanation: If lengthening a timeout could break your invariants, the protocol is unsafe. The timeout only ever trades detection latency against false-positive rate.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain, in terms of the $\Omega$ abstraction, why Raft's randomised election timeout in the range $[T, {k}T]$ is a liveness mechanism and not a safety mechanism.
L4.answer: $\Omega$ requires that eventually exactly one correct process is trusted as leader everywhere. Randomisation makes split votes independent across rounds, so the probability of $r$ consecutive split elections decays geometrically and a single candidate eventually times out first. Safety comes from terms and one-vote-per-term, which hold under any timeout values.
L4.explanation: This is the precise sense in which Raft does not violate FLP: it can in principle split-vote forever, a liveness failure with probability zero under randomisation, but it can never elect two leaders in one term.

L0.body:
Fischer, Lynch, Paterson 1985. The theorem, stated exactly:

  MODEL   asynchronous message passing, reliable channels, deterministic processes
  FAULTS  at most one process may crash
  CLAIM   no protocol satisfies all three of
            agreement    no two correct processes decide differently
            validity     the decision is some process's input
            termination  every correct process eventually decides

Drop termination and consensus is trivially solvable. That is the loophole every real system uses.
L0.cloze:
MODEL: {{c1::asynchronous}}, reliable channels, {{c2::deterministic}} processes
FAULTS: at most {{c3::one}} crash
No protocol gives agreement, validity and {{c4::termination}} together.
Real systems escape by weakening {{c5::termination}}.

concepts.L1: In an asynchronous system with even one crash failure, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus. Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985.
concepts.L2: The escape is that FLP forbids guaranteed termination, not consensus itself. Real systems escape via randomization (Ben-Or) or partial synchrony assumptions (failure detectors, timeouts). Raft doesn't violate FLP — it can theoretically livelock in leader election, and randomized timeouts make that vanishingly unlikely.
concepts.L3: The proof is a strategy for an adversarial scheduler, not a counting argument. Call a reachable configuration bivalent if both decision values are still reachable from it. Step one: some initial configuration is bivalent, shown by walking a chain of initial states differing in one input; adjacent 0-valent and 1-valent states cannot be adjacent once one process's crash makes them indistinguishable. Step two: from any bivalent configuration the scheduler can deliver some pending message and land in another bivalent one, because if every successor were univalent, two would differ only in the order of two independent events. Iterate forever: an infinite run with no decision.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor claims their consensus protocol 'always terminates, tolerates {f} crash failures, and makes no timing assumptions'. Identify which of the three FLP conditions the claim must actually be violating, and name the two standard escapes.
L4.answer: The claim is false as stated; with $f \geq 1$ and no timing assumptions, guaranteed termination is impossible. The escapes are randomisation, which gives termination with probability 1 rather than certainty (Ben-Or), and partial synchrony, which gives termination only after an unknown Global Stabilisation Time (Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer).
L4.explanation: FLP bans guaranteed deterministic termination in the asynchronous model. Any real protocol either randomises, assumes eventual timing, or quietly redefines terminate.

L4.prompt_tpl: FLP assumes at most {f} crash failure and reliable channels. Explain why strengthening the model to reliable channels and only one fault makes the result stronger rather than weaker.
L4.answer: An impossibility proved under the most generous assumptions holds a fortiori under harsher ones. Because it needs only one crash and never drops a message, no amount of network reliability or fault-count reduction rescues you; only changing the timing model or dropping determinism does.
L4.explanation: Read impossibility results by their assumptions: weak assumptions make a possibility result strong, and strong assumptions make an impossibility result strong. FLP is the second kind.

L0.body:
Definitions used by the proof, over configurations $C$ (all process states plus the message buffer):

  $C$ is 0-valent   every reachable decision from $C$ is 0
  $C$ is 1-valent   every reachable decision from $C$ is 1
  $C$ is bivalent   both are still reachable

  Lemma 1  some initial configuration is bivalent
  Lemma 2  from any bivalent $C$ and any pending message $m$,
           there is a run applying $m$ that ends bivalent
  Corollary  the adversary schedules forever; no decision is ever reached
L0.cloze:
$C$ is {{c1::bivalent}} when both decisions are still reachable.
  Lemma 1: some {{c2::initial}} configuration is bivalent.
  Lemma 2: from any bivalent $C$ the adversary can apply any pending message and stay {{c3::bivalent}}.
  Together they build an {{c4::infinite}} run with no decision.

concepts.L1: The machinery behind FLP. A configuration is bivalent if the protocol has not yet committed to an outcome. The proof shows bivalence is both reachable initially and indefinitely preservable by an adversarial message scheduler.
concepts.L2: The adversary never crashes anyone. It only delays one message, and delay is free in the asynchronous model. People remember FLP as being about failures; the single permitted crash is used purely to make two configurations indistinguishable in Lemma 1, and the infinite run itself is crash-free.
concepts.L3: Lemma 1: line up initial configurations $I_0, \ldots, I_n$ where $I_k$ has the first $k$ inputs set to 1. $I_0$ decides 0, $I_n$ decides 1, so somewhere adjacent $I_k$ and $I_{k+1}$ differ in valency while differing only in process $p$'s input. Crash $p$ at the start: the two runs are then identical to everyone else, so they must decide the same, contradiction unless one of them is bivalent. Lemma 2: suppose every configuration reached from bivalent $C$ after delivering $m$ is univalent. Events on distinct processes commute, so applying two of them in either order reaches the same configuration, forcing their valencies to agree. That contradiction leaves some successor bivalent.

L4.prompt_tpl: In Lemma 1 the proof crashes exactly {f} process. Explain precisely what that crash buys, and why the lemma fails without it.
L4.answer: Crashing the one process whose input differs makes the two adjacent initial configurations indistinguishable to every remaining process, so any correct protocol must produce the same decision in both. That forces the contradiction with them having different valencies. Without a crash the other processes could read $p$'s input and legitimately decide differently.
L4.explanation: This is why FLP needs a fault at all: not to disrupt the run, but to create indistinguishability between two configurations that would otherwise be separable.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague summarises FLP as 'consensus is impossible if {n} node can fail'. Give the two words their summary is missing and explain what each one is doing.
L4.answer: Asynchronous and guaranteed (or deterministic and terminating). Asynchronous: with partial synchrony consensus is solvable. Guaranteed termination: consensus with probability 1, or eventual termination after GST, is solvable. Agreement and validity are never at risk.
L4.explanation: The folk statement drops both qualifiers and becomes false. Raft, Paxos and Zab all solve consensus with crash faults; they simply cannot promise a bound on when.

L0.body:
Gilbert and Lynch 2002, Theorem 1, in the asynchronous network model:

  it is impossible to implement a read/write register that is both
    available          every request to a non-failed node returns a non-error response
    atomic (linearizable)
  in all fair executions in which arbitrary messages may be lost.

The partition is an assumption of the theorem, not a third choice.
L0.cloze:
CAP's C is specifically {{c1::linearizability}}; its A is {{c2::every request to a non-failed node returns}}.
Partitions are an {{c3::assumption}}, not a choice.
The formal statement is due to {{c4::Gilbert and Lynch}}, 2002.

concepts.L1: During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency (linearizability) and availability. That's it.
concepts.L2: CAP is not 'pick two of three.' Partitions are a fact of networks, not a choice. And the C in CAP is specifically linearizability — a system can be 'consistent' in other senses while being AP. Brewer himself wrote a retrospective saying the 2-of-3 formulation is misleading.
concepts.L3: The proof needs three nodes and two messages. Partition the network into $G_1$ and $G_2$ with all messages between them lost. A client writes $v_1$ to a node in $G_1$; availability forces that write to return success without hearing from $G_2$. A client then reads from a node in $G_2$; availability forces a response, and that node has no way to learn $v_1$, so it returns the old value. That read is not linearizable, since it is ordered after a completed write yet does not see it. Hence availability plus linearizability plus partition tolerance is unachievable. Note what it does not say: nothing about latency absent a partition, nothing about weaker models, nothing about two of three.

L4.prompt_tpl: A three-node cluster splits into a majority side of {a} nodes and a minority side of {b}. Under a CP design, state exactly which side serves reads, which serves writes, and what the minority side returns; then state what changes under an AP design.
L4.answer: CP: the majority side of 2 serves both reads and writes; the minority node returns an error or blocks, because it cannot form a quorum of 2 out of 3. AP: both sides accept reads and writes, the minority node returns possibly stale data, and the two sides must reconcile divergent versions on heal, typically with version vectors or last-write-wins.
L4.explanation: The CP system sacrifices availability on the minority side only, not globally. That is the most common misreading: a CP system is fully available whenever a quorum is reachable.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rank these claims as true or false and justify: (a) 'we chose AP so we gave up consistency entirely', (b) 'we chose CA because our datacenter network is reliable', (c) 'CAP forbids a system that is linearizable and available {pct}% of the time'.
L4.answer: (a) False: an AP system can still be causally consistent or offer session guarantees; only linearizability is surrendered. (b) False: CA is not an option, partitions occur whether or not you plan for them; a CA design is a CP design that has not thought about the partition. (c) False: CAP constrains behaviour only during a partition, so a linearizable system is available whenever no partition is active.
L4.explanation: Brewer's own 2012 retrospective calls the two-of-three formulation misleading for exactly these reasons.

concepts.L1: If Partition, then Availability or Consistency; Else, Latency or Consistency. Abadi's extension, and the more useful formulation.
concepts.L2: The 'else' branch is the one that matters daily — partitions are rare, but the latency/consistency tradeoff is paid on every single request. Most system design discussions should be about PACELC's else clause and instead they're about CAP.
concepts.L3: The else-branch is quantifiable, which is what makes PACELC more useful than CAP. Linearizable reads require contacting a quorum, so their latency is bounded below by the round-trip to the median-distance replica. Replicas in Virginia, Ireland and Singapore make a quorum read from Virginia cost the Virginia-Ireland round trip, roughly 75 to 90 ms, against under 1 ms served locally and stale. Spanner pays this consciously and adds commit-wait on top. Dynamo-style stores set $R = W = 1$ and pay nothing, accepting that a read may miss a just-acknowledged write. Partitions might cost you an hour a year; the else-branch costs you tens of milliseconds on every single request, forever.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three replicas sit in regions with pairwise round-trip times of {a} ms, {b} ms and {c} ms. A client colocated with replica 1 issues a linearizable read requiring a majority quorum. Give the minimum added latency versus a local stale read, and explain which link determines it. Answer with the minimum added latency in milliseconds.
L4.answer: The quorum is 2 of 3, and replica 1 counts itself, so it needs one remote acknowledgement: the minimum is the smaller of the two round trips from replica 1. With links 1-2 = a and 1-3 = b, the added latency is min(a, b) ms. For a=70, b=90 that is 70 ms; for a=150, b=200 it is 150 ms. The 2-3 link never binds for a client at replica 1.
L4.explanation: Majority quorums are cheaper than people assume because the coordinator counts itself: with $n=3$ you wait for the nearest peer, not the farthest. With $n=5$ you wait for the second-nearest.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a shopping cart, a bank ledger, and a session store, give the PACELC classification you would target and one sentence of justification each, assuming a {r}-region deployment.
L4.answer: Cart: PA/EL, since add-to-cart must never fail and merge-on-heal is acceptable with an add-wins set. Ledger: PC/EC, since a double-spend is unrecoverable and the else-branch latency is worth paying. Session store: PA/EL with sticky routing and read-your-writes, since staleness is invisible if the user is pinned.
L4.explanation: The lesson of PACELC is that these three deserve different answers, and that the else-branch, not the partition branch, is where the difference is felt.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a system can be PA/EC, and name a system with that classification and the {n}-node configuration in which it shows up.
L4.answer: PA/EC means it prefers availability under partition but consistency in the normal case. MongoDB with default write concern and primary reads behaves this way: reads from the primary are consistent absent a partition, while failover and rollback windows can expose divergence during one. The two branches are independent knobs.
L4.explanation: The four combinations are all realisable. PA/EC is common in systems where the normal path routes through a single primary but failover is optimistic.

concepts.t: The two generals and the coordinated attack

L0.body:
The setup: two generals on facing hills, a messenger who may be captured, and a need to attack simultaneously.

  A -> B: "attack at dawn"          A does not know it arrived
  B -> A: "ack: attack at dawn"     B does not know the ack arrived
  A -> B: "ack the ack"             A still does not know
  ...

Induction: take any protocol with the fewest messages that works.
The last message cannot have been necessary, since its loss is undetectable
to the sender. Delete it. Repeat until zero messages remain. Contradiction.
L0.cloze: The proof is by {{c1::induction on the number of messages}}: the {{c2::last}} message cannot matter, since its {{c3::loss is undetectable to the sender}}. What is unattainable in finite messages is {{c4::common knowledge}}.

concepts.L1: No finite protocol over an unreliable channel achieves common knowledge. Implies exactly-once delivery is impossible.
concepts.L2: The practical consequence: 'exactly-once' in Kafka or anywhere else is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing plus deduplication with a persistent key. Vendors market this as exactly-once; being able to explain what's really happening is a strong signal.
concepts.L3: The object being denied is common knowledge: not just 'both know', but 'both know that both know', without end. Each message adds exactly one level of mutual knowledge and never reaches the limit. In a queue: the producer sends, the broker persists, the ack is lost, the producer retries, and the broker holds two copies. No protocol over a lossy channel prevents this: a lost message and a lost ack are indistinguishable to the sender. The only fix is receiver-side: a stable persistent dedup key. Kafka's exactly-once is a producer id and sequence number checked at the broker plus transactional offset commits, which is at-least-once delivery with server-side dedup.

L4.prompt_tpl: Suppose a protocol delivers coordinated attack using exactly {k} messages over a channel that may drop any message. Show the contradiction by considering the final message.
L4.answer: Take a shortest correct protocol with k messages. Its sender cannot know whether the k-th message arrived, so the sender must attack whether or not it was delivered. But then the protocol still works with that message deleted, contradicting minimality of k. By induction the protocol needs zero messages, which cannot coordinate two independent inputs.
L4.explanation: The induction is the entire proof and it needs no probability. Note it fails immediately if the channel is reliable, or if the generals are allowed to attack at different times.

L4.prompt_tpl: A payments API promises exactly-once charge creation. It is called {n} times with the same request due to client retries. Describe the minimum machinery that makes the promise true, and state the one thing that machinery cannot survive.
L4.answer: A client-supplied idempotency key, persisted atomically with the charge in the same transaction, plus a rule that a repeated key returns the stored response rather than performing new work. It cannot survive the key being retained for less time than the client's maximum retry horizon: once the record is evicted, a late retry creates a duplicate.
L4.explanation: Exactly-once effects are achievable; exactly-once delivery is not. The gap is bridged by a durable dedup record, and its retention window is the real parameter.

L0.body:
Three generals, one traitor. Oral messages only. Commander $C$, lieutenants $L_1$, $L_2$.

Case A, traitor is the commander:
  $C \to L_1$: "attack"      $C \to L_2$: "retreat"
  $L_1 \to L_2$: "he said attack"   $L_2 \to L_1$: "he said retreat"
  $L_1$ sees (attack, retreat). $L_2$ sees (retreat, attack).

Case B, traitor is $L_2$:
  $C \to$ both: "attack"     $L_2 \to L_1$: "he said retreat"
  $L_1$ sees (attack, retreat) -- identical to Case A.

$L_1$ cannot distinguish A from B, so $n = 3$ cannot tolerate $f = 1$.
L0.cloze: With $n=3$ and one traitor, $L_1$'s view in the {{c1::traitor-commander}} case is identical to its view in the {{c2::traitor-lieutenant}} case, so no decision rule is correct in both. Oral messages therefore need $n \geq$ {{c3::3f+1}}; with {{c4::signed}} messages the bound disappears.

concepts.L1: Lamport, Shostak and Pease 1982. Agreement among processes that may lie, and lie inconsistently to different peers. The impossibility for $n \leq 3f$ with unauthenticated messages, and the $3f+1$ construction that works.
concepts.L2: The bound is about unforgeable attribution, not about counting liars. With digital signatures a lieutenant cannot misreport what the commander said, the two cases above become distinguishable, and agreement is possible for any $f$. Signatures buy you the impossibility result's premise, not just convenience.
concepts.L3: The scenario above is the whole impossibility proof, scaled by a partitioning argument: group $3f$ processes into three sets of $f$, let one set be faulty, and simulate the three-general case with one process per set. Since the three-process case is unsolvable, so is the $3f$ case. The positive direction, algorithm OM($f$), recurses: the commander sends its value, then each lieutenant acts as commander of an OM($f-1$) among the remaining $n-1$, and each process takes the majority of what it gathers. Cost is $O(n^{f+1})$ messages, which is why PBFT replaced it with a three-phase, signature-assisted protocol at $O(n^{2})$ per request in the common case.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need Byzantine agreement tolerating $f = {f}$ faulty nodes with oral messages. Give $n$, the quorum size, the size of the intersection of any two quorums, and how many honest nodes that intersection is guaranteed to contain. Answer with the size of the intersection of any two quorums.
L4.answer: $n = 3f+1$, quorum $q = 2f+1$, intersection $2q - n = 2(2f+1) - (3f+1) = f+1$, of which at most $f$ are faulty, so at least 1 is honest. For $f=1$: 4, 3, 2, 1. For $f=2$: 7, 5, 3, 1. For $f=3$: 10, 7, 4, 1. For $f=5$: 16, 11, 6, 1.
L4.explanation: The design target is exactly one guaranteed honest witness in every quorum intersection. That single node is what carries a committed value forward across views.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your {n}-node service runs entirely inside one company's VPC, all nodes running the same binary from the same build. Argue for or against Byzantine fault tolerance, and name the specific failure class BFT would and would not have caught.
L4.answer: Against. BFT triples replica cost and adds rounds to defend against an adversary you do not have inside a trust boundary. It would catch a compromised node or a memory-corruption-induced lie, but not the dominant real cause of divergence: a deterministic bug in the shared binary, which BFT cannot detect because every replica computes the same wrong answer.
L4.explanation: The correlated-bug argument is the strongest case against BFT inside one organisation. BFT assumes independent failures; identical binaries fail identically.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain how adding unforgeable signatures changes the {n}-node bound, and why the change is about information rather than about trust.
L4.answer: With signatures, a relayed message carries proof of its origin, so a lieutenant cannot claim the commander said something it did not. The two indistinguishable cases become distinguishable, the impossibility argument collapses, and agreement is achievable with $n \geq f+2$ (SM algorithms). The gain is that each process now learns strictly more from the same messages.
L4.explanation: Lamport's paper proves both directions. The unauthenticated bound $3f+1$ is a bound on what can be inferred from unattributable hearsay, not a bound on adversary strength.

concepts.t: Consensus and atomic broadcast are equivalent

L0.body:
Two problems, one difficulty.

  consensus         one value, agreed by all correct processes
  atomic broadcast  a stream of messages, delivered to all correct
                    processes in the SAME total order

Reductions in both directions:
  atomic broadcast -> consensus: broadcast your proposal, decide the first delivered
  consensus -> atomic broadcast: run consensus instance $k$ to decide the $k$-th
                                 batch of the delivered sequence

So a replicated state machine is exactly an atomic broadcast of commands.
L0.cloze:
Atomic broadcast delivers messages to all correct processes in the same {{c1::total order}}.
From atomic broadcast, decide the {{c2::first}} message delivered.
From consensus, run instance {{c3::k}} to decide the k-th batch.
A replicated state machine is atomic broadcast of {{c4::commands}} applied to a {{c5::deterministic}} state machine.

concepts.L1: Chandra and Toueg's reduction: solving either problem solves the other. Total-order broadcast is a sequence of consensus instances, and consensus is one instance of total-order broadcast. Everything FLP forbids for one is forbidden for the other.
concepts.L2: The equivalence is why Multi-Paxos and Raft look the way they do: both are ordered logs, not repeated single-value agreements. It also tells you the hard part is not agreeing on a value, it is agreeing on a sequence, and hence that the log, not the leader, is the primary abstraction.
concepts.L3: Lamport's state-machine replication recipe follows directly: if every replica starts in the same state and applies the same deterministic commands in the same order, all replicas hold the same state. Ordering the commands is atomic broadcast; atomic broadcast is consensus; so replication inherits FLP. Two practical consequences. First, determinism is a correctness requirement, not a style preference: a command that reads the local clock, iterates a hash map, or calls rand() will diverge replicas even with a perfect log. Second, batching is free ordering: instance $k$ can decide a whole batch, so throughput scales with batch size while the round count stays fixed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A replicated key-value store applies commands from an agreed log. One command is SET expiry = now() + {ttl}. Replicas diverge within hours. Identify the bug and give the standard fix.
L4.answer: now() is evaluated at apply time on each replica, so each computes a different expiry from its own clock. The state machine is non-deterministic, which breaks the state-machine replication premise. Fix: evaluate the timestamp once, at the leader, before the command enters the log, and replicate the resolved absolute value.
L4.explanation: The rule is that all non-determinism (clocks, randomness, iteration order, external calls) must be resolved into the log entry before replication, never at apply time.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given a working atomic broadcast primitive, construct a consensus protocol for {n} processes in three lines, and state which consensus property each line establishes.
L4.answer: 1. Each process atomically broadcasts its proposed value: gives validity, since every candidate decision is some process's input. 2. Each process decides the value of the first message it delivers: gives agreement, because all correct processes deliver in the same total order and therefore see the same first message. 3. Termination follows from atomic broadcast's own delivery guarantee.
L4.explanation: The reduction is short because total order is the hard part. Its cost is that atomic broadcast inherits FLP: no asynchronous implementation can guarantee step 3.

L0.body:
A history is linearizable iff you can pick one point inside each operation's interval
such that the resulting sequential order is legal for the object.

  A: |--- write(x,1) ---|
  B:        |--- read(x) -> 0 ---|

B's read overlaps A's write, so returning 0 is LEGAL: choose B's point before A's.

  A: |-- write(x,1) --|
  B:                      |-- read(x) -> 0 --|

B starts after A returns. Returning 0 is a linearizability VIOLATION.
L0.cloze:
Pick one {{c1::linearization point}} inside each operation's interval so the sequential order is legal.
Overlapping operations may be ordered {{c2::either way}}.
A read that starts strictly {{c3::after}} a write returns must see it.
Linearizability is a {{c4::single-object}} guarantee and it is {{c5::composable}}.

concepts.L1: Every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and response, consistent with real time. A single-object guarantee, and composable — a system of linearizable objects is linearizable.
concepts.L2: Composability is the property that makes linearizability worth its cost. Serializability is not composable in the same way, which is one reason the two are different guarantees rather than the same guarantee at different layers.
concepts.L3: The real-time constraint is what makes the two diagrams above differ, and it is the only difference. Composability follows from locality: Herlihy and Wing prove that a history is linearizable iff its restriction to each object is linearizable. So you can implement each register, queue and lock independently, verify each in isolation, and the composed system is linearizable with no extra coordination. Nothing analogous holds for serializability: two individually serializable stores can compose into a non-serializable execution. Locality is the whole practical argument for paying linearizability's cost only on the objects that need it.

L4.prompt_tpl: History: A does write(x,{v}) from t=0 to t=10. B does read(x) from t=4 to t=14 and returns 0. C does read(x) from t=12 to t=20 and returns 0. Which read, if either, violates linearizability, and why?
L4.answer: C violates it. B overlaps the write, so a linearization point for B before A's is legal. C begins at t=12, after the write returned at t=10, so every legal ordering places C after the write; returning 0 means it missed a completed write. Note that B returning 0 and C returning the value would also be legal, but B returning the value and C returning 0 would not.
L4.explanation: The second half is the subtle part: linearizability also forbids going backwards. Once any operation observes the new value, no later operation may observe the old one.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {n} independently linearizable services. A client writes to service 1, then reads from service 2. Is the composed system linearizable? Justify using the locality theorem and say what breaks the guarantee in practice.
L4.answer: Formally yes: linearizability is local, so a composition of linearizable objects is linearizable, and the client's own program order plus real time orders the two calls. What breaks in practice is that the client's write to service 1 does not causally reach service 2 unless the client itself carries the dependency, so cross-service invariants still need a transaction or a shared log.
L4.explanation: Locality gives you per-object composability, not multi-object atomicity. Those are different guarantees and conflating them is the standard error.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cache serves reads from a local replica with at most {ms} ms of lag behind a linearizable primary. State precisely which linearizability requirement is violated and give a minimal history.
L4.answer: The real-time requirement. History: client X writes v and receives the ack at t=0; client Y reads at t=1 ms from the lagging replica and gets the pre-write value. Y's read began strictly after X's write completed, so no legal linearization exists. The system is at best sequentially consistent, and typically only eventually consistent.
L4.explanation: This is why any read-replica offload is a consistency decision, not a performance decision. The lag bound tells you the staleness anomaly window exactly.

concepts.t: A history that separates the models

L0.body:
One history, three verdicts. Two objects $x$ and $y$, both start at 0.

  T1: write(x,1); commit          real time: [0, 10]
  T2: read(x) -> 0; write(y,1)    real time: [20, 30]

SERIALIZABLE?    yes -- the serial order T2 then T1 produces exactly this result
LINEARIZABLE?    n/a -- linearizability is per-object; per object each is fine
STRICT SERIALIZABLE? no -- T2 starts after T1 commits, so T1 must precede T2,
                     and in that order T2's read must return 1
L0.cloze:
T2 reads the pre-T1 value even though it {{c1::started after T1 committed}}.
This history is {{c2::serializable}} (order T2 before T1) but not {{c3::strict serializable}}.
The property serializability lacks is the {{c4::real-time}} constraint.

concepts.L1: The concrete two-transaction history that makes the words mean something. Serializability allows any equivalent serial order, including one that contradicts wall-clock reality; strict serializability additionally requires the serial order to respect real-time precedence.
concepts.L2: The stale read is not a bug in the database, it is inside serializability's definition. This is why 'we use SERIALIZABLE isolation' does not answer the question 'can a read see stale data', and why Jepsen tests strict serializability rather than serializability when it can.
concepts.L3: Run the history. T1 commits at $t=10$. T2 runs from $t=20$ to $t=30$ and reads $x=0$. Is there an equivalent serial schedule? Yes: T2 then T1. In that schedule T2 reads $x=0$ (correct, T1 has not run) and writes $y=1$; then T1 writes $x=1$. Final state $x=1$, $y=1$, matching. So the history is serializable. Now add the real-time axiom: if T1 commits before T2 begins, every valid order must place T1 first. Under that order T2's read of $x$ must return 1, which it did not, so the history is not strict serializable. Snapshot isolation admits this history too, plus write skew, which is why SI is neither serializable nor comparable to it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Construct a history over two keys in which transaction T2 begins {gap} seconds after T1 commits, yet the history is serializable. State the equivalent serial order and the property it violates.
L4.answer: T1: write(x,1), commit. T2 (begins later): read(x) returns 0, write(y,1), commit. Equivalent serial order: T2, then T1. It violates strict serializability, since real time forces T1 before T2 and in that order T2's read must return 1. The gap length is irrelevant, which is the point.
L4.explanation: Serializability constrains only the existence of some equivalent serial order. Real-time precedence is an extra axiom that only strict serializability adds.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor advertises 'serializable, {nines} nines available across regions'. What single follow-up question separates a genuinely strong system from one that will serve you hour-old reads, and what answer are you looking for?
L4.answer: Ask whether it is strict serializable, that is, whether a transaction that begins after another commits is guaranteed to observe it. The answer you want names either a real-time constraint or an external-consistency mechanism such as commit-wait or a leader lease. Anything that only cites an equivalent serial order permits arbitrarily stale reads.
L4.explanation: Spanner says external consistency, which is strict serializability. CockroachDB says serializable with a linearizability caveat on stale-read modes. The distinction is exactly what this question surfaces.

L0.body:
A schedule is serializable iff it is equivalent to SOME serial execution.

  T1: r(x) w(x)
  T2:        r(y) w(y)

Conflict-serializability test: build the precedence graph. Add an edge $T_i \to T_j$
whenever $T_i$ accesses an item before $T_j$ and at least one access is a write.
The schedule is conflict-serializable iff that graph is ACYCLIC.

No node in that graph carries a timestamp. Real time never appears.
L0.cloze:
Serializable means equivalent to {{c1::some}} serial execution.
The conflict test builds a {{c2::precedence graph}} and checks it is {{c3::acyclic}}.
The definition mentions real time {{c4::never}}, which is why serializable systems may serve {{c5::stale}} reads.

concepts.L1: A transaction-level guarantee: some serial order of transactions produces the same result. Says nothing about real-time ordering.
concepts.L2: Serializable but not linearizable systems can serve stale reads — a transaction can be ordered before one that committed an hour ago. Strict serializability is the combination, and it's what Spanner provides.
concepts.L3: Draw the precedence graph for a schedule with an anomaly and the mechanism is visible. Serializability is a graph-acyclicity condition over conflicts, and acyclicity says nothing about when the transactions ran. The useful framing: serializability is the multi-object atomicity dimension, linearizability the recency dimension, and they are orthogonal, so neither implies the other. A linearizable register is not serializable, having no transactions; a serializable database with follower reads is not linearizable. Strict serializability is their conjunction, and most consistency confusion is one word doing both jobs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Schedule over items x and y with {n} transactions: T1 reads x; T2 writes x; T2 writes y; T1 writes y. Build the precedence graph and state whether the schedule is conflict-serializable.
L4.answer: Edges: T1 reads x before T2 writes x, giving T1 to T2. T2 writes y before T1 writes y, giving T2 to T1. The graph has a cycle T1 to T2 to T1, so the schedule is not conflict-serializable. This is the classic write-skew-adjacent cycle that two-phase locking prevents and snapshot isolation does not.
L4.explanation: The precedence-graph test is mechanical and worth being able to run in your head: one edge per conflicting pair, in access order, then look for a cycle.

L4.prompt_tpl: True or false, with justification: (a) linearizable implies serializable, (b) serializable implies linearizable, (c) a system offering both is called strict serializable, (d) a {n}-node serializable system can return a value written {age} minutes ago as the newest value.
L4.answer: (a) False: linearizability is a single-object recency property with no transaction concept. (b) False: serializability has no real-time constraint. (c) True. (d) True: a transaction may be ordered before an older committed one, so an arbitrarily stale read is permitted by the definition.
L4.explanation: The two guarantees are on orthogonal axes, atomicity across objects versus recency in real time. Neither implies the other, and their conjunction has its own name.

L0.body:
Strict serializability $=$ serializability $+$ linearizability's real-time order.

  serializable        some equivalent serial order exists
  strict serializable that serial order also respects real-time precedence:
                      if $T_i$ commits before $T_j$ begins, $T_i$ precedes $T_j$

Spanner calls this EXTERNAL CONSISTENCY and buys it with commit-wait:

  commit_ts = TT.now().latest
  wait until TT.now().earliest > commit_ts    // about $2\epsilon$, roughly 5-7 ms
  release locks
L0.cloze:
Strict serializability adds the {{c1::real-time}} order to serializability.
Spanner calls it {{c2::external consistency}}.
It is bought with {{c3::commit-wait}}: wait until TT.now().earliest exceeds the commit timestamp,
about {{c4::2 epsilon}}, roughly 5 to 7 ms.

concepts.L1: The conjunction of the two strong models: multi-object transactions that are equivalent to a serial order, and that order agrees with wall-clock reality. It is the strongest practical guarantee a distributed database offers.
concepts.L2: It is not free and rarely the default. Spanner pays a mandatory commit-wait of roughly twice the TrueTime uncertainty on every read-write transaction. CockroachDB does not offer it by default, giving serializable plus per-key linearizability with a documented anomaly for causally-unrelated transactions.
concepts.L3: Why real time needs hardware. To place transactions in a real-time-consistent order you need timestamps whose ordering implies real-time ordering. Local clocks disagree by tens of milliseconds under NTP, so a naive timestamp order can invert reality. Spanner makes the uncertainty explicit: TrueTime returns an interval of width $2\epsilon$, typically 1 to 7 ms, and the commit protocol waits it out before releasing locks. After the wait the commit timestamp is definitely in the past everywhere, so any later transaction gets a strictly larger one. The cost is a floor on write latency.

L4.prompt_tpl: TrueTime reports an uncertainty half-width $\epsilon$ of {eps} ms. Give the expected commit-wait for one read-write transaction, and the maximum sustained rate of dependent serial transactions on one key. Answer with the expected commit-wait in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Commit-wait is about $2\epsilon$: 2 ms, 8 ms and 14 ms respectively. Dependent serial transactions on one key are bounded by roughly $1/(2\epsilon)$ per second, ignoring all other costs: about 500, 125 and 71 per second. Independent transactions on different keys are unaffected, since commit-wait overlaps with Paxos communication.
L4.explanation: The Spanner paper measures $\epsilon$ as a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms and commit-wait at about 5 ms. The bound only binds a serial dependency chain on one key, not aggregate throughput.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your team needs a {t}-region ledger. Argue for strict serializability or against it, naming the specific anomaly you accept if you choose plain serializability.
L4.answer: For, if two ledger entries can be causally linked outside the database (a user sees a confirmation, then queries balance from another region). The anomaly you accept under plain serializability is a transaction beginning after another commits yet not observing it, so a customer can see a confirmed transfer and then a balance that predates it. If all access flows through one region and one connection, session guarantees may suffice at far lower cost.
L4.explanation: The decision hinges on whether out-of-band causality exists. Where clients only ever talk to the database, session guarantees are cheaper and sufficient.

prereqs: A history that separates the models

L0.body:
Lamport 1979, the definition used in both hardware and distributed systems:

  the result of any execution is the same as if the operations of all processors
  were executed in some sequential order, and the operations of each individual
  processor appear in that sequence in the order specified by its program.

  P1: W(x,1)
  P2:              R(x) -> 0     R(x) -> 1

LEGAL under sequential consistency (P2's first read is ordered before W).
ILLEGAL under linearizability if that read began after W returned.
L0.cloze:
Sequential consistency requires a single {{c1::total order}} that respects each process's {{c2::program order}}.
It does NOT require agreement with {{c3::real time}}.
Adding the real-time constraint gives {{c4::linearizability}}.

concepts.L1: All processes see the same order of operations, consistent with each process's program order, but not necessarily real time.
concepts.L2: The distinction from linearizability is exactly the real-time constraint. This is the same distinction as in the hardware memory model chapter, and noticing that the two fields independently derived the same hierarchy is a nice observation.
concepts.L3: The two fields converged because the problem is the same: many agents, one apparent order, no shared clock. In hardware, x86 TSO is not sequentially consistent because store buffers let a core's own store become visible to itself before others see it; the fix, an mfence or a locked instruction, is a store-buffer drain that costs tens of cycles. In a distributed store the equivalent is a follower serving reads from a consistent prefix of the log: every client sees the same order, but any client can be arbitrarily far behind. Sequential consistency is also not composable, which is exactly the property linearizability has and this one lacks.

L4.prompt_tpl: A follower serves reads from a consistent prefix of the replicated log, lagging by up to {ms} ms. Argue whether this is sequentially consistent, linearizable, both or neither, for a client pinned to that follower.
L4.answer: Sequentially consistent for a pinned client: all clients observe the same log order and each client's own operations appear in program order. Not linearizable: a read starting after another client's write completes may return the old value, violating real time. If the client can switch followers it loses even sequential consistency, since it may go backwards in the log.
L4.explanation: The pinning condition is what makes this work, and it is exactly the sticky-session trick. Losing affinity loses the guarantee.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why sequential consistency is not composable, using {n} objects and a two-process history.
L4.answer: Take objects x and y. P1 writes x then reads y (gets 0); P2 writes y then reads x (gets 0). Each object in isolation admits a sequential order consistent with program order. Together, x's order forces P1's write before P2's read failing, and symmetrically for y, so no single total order respects both program orders. The composite history is therefore not sequentially consistent although each object's projection is.
L4.explanation: This is Dekker's example. Linearizability's locality theorem is precisely the property that fails here, and it is why linearizability, not sequential consistency, is the composable one.

L0.body:
Delivery rule for a causally consistent store, using a vector clock $V$:

  on receive(update $u$ from $j$ with clock $V_u$) at node $i$:
      wait until   $V_u[j] = V_i[j] + 1$              // $u$ is the next update from $j$
            and    $V_u[k] \leq V_i[k]$ for all $k \neq j$   // all its dependencies are here
      apply $u$;   $V_i[j] \mathrel{+}= 1$

Updates are buffered, never rejected. No coordination, no quorum, no leader.
L0.cloze:
An update is delivered only when $V_u[j] = V_i[j] + $ {{c1::1}} and $V_u[k] \leq V_i[k]$ for all other $k$.
Out-of-order updates are {{c2::buffered}}, not rejected.
The protocol needs no {{c3::coordination}}, which is why it stays {{c4::available}} under partition.

concepts.L1: Operations related by happens-before are seen in that order by everyone; concurrent operations may be seen in any order. The strongest model available under partition while remaining available.
concepts.L2: This is a genuinely important result (Mahajan et al.) and it's underused. Causal+ consistency gives you a lot of what people want from strong consistency without giving up availability, and most 'we need strong consistency' requirements are actually causal requirements.
concepts.L3: The availability result is what makes this the interesting model. Attiya and Welch, and later Mahajan, Alvisi and Dahlin, show causal consistency (with convergence, hence causal+) is the strongest model achievable by an always-available, one-way-convergent system: strictly stronger models require blocking during a partition. The delivery rule shows why: a node waits only for updates it will eventually receive, never for a remote acknowledgement, so no client request blocks on the network. A linearizable read must contact a quorum and therefore fails on the minority side. The gap: causal consistency does not order concurrent writes, so you still need a merge policy.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team says 'we need strong consistency' because a user must never see a reply to a comment before the comment. Diagnose the actual requirement and give the cheapest mechanism, assuming {n} regions.
L4.answer: The requirement is causal, not linearizable: the reply causally depends on the comment, so causal delivery suffices. Cheapest mechanism is to attach the comment's version (a dot or a compact dependency set) to the reply and have replicas buffer the reply until that version is applied. No quorum, no leader, no availability loss under partition.
L4.explanation: Most stated strong-consistency requirements are causal requirements. Naming the difference converts a global-coordination design into a metadata design.

L4.prompt_tpl: A causally consistent store buffers an update until its dependencies arrive. Under a partition lasting {min} minutes, one node's buffer grows without bound and it eventually OOMs. Is causal consistency at fault? What is the real defect?
L4.answer: Causal consistency is not at fault; buffering is inherent to the delivery rule. The defect is an unbounded queue with no admission control. The fix is a bounded buffer plus a fallback: shed or reject new updates, or switch to a state transfer and resynchronise from a snapshot once the dependency chain exceeds a threshold.
L4.explanation: This is the same unbounded-queue failure mode as elsewhere in the domain. Every wait-until rule needs a bound and a defined behaviour at the bound.

Terry et al.'s session guarantees, plus the staleness bounds:

  read-your-writes   a read sees all writes previously made in this session
  monotonic reads    successive reads never go backwards in time
  monotonic writes   a session's writes are applied in the order issued
  writes-follow-reads a write is ordered after the writes the session read

  bounded staleness  reads lag the latest write by at most $t$ seconds
                     or at most $k$ versions

Implementation: carry the session's highest version in a token; route or wait
until a replica has caught up to it.
L0.cloze:
The four session guarantees are read-your-writes, {{c1::monotonic reads}}, monotonic writes and {{c2::writes-follow-reads}}.
Together they imply {{c3::causal}} consistency for a single session.
The standard implementation carries the session's {{c4::highest seen version}} in a token.

concepts.L1: Session guarantees. Weaker than causal but often sufficient, and much cheaper.
concepts.L2: Most user-facing consistency complaints are read-your-writes violations specifically. Sticky sessions or a write timestamp in a cookie solves the perceived problem without any global coordination.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is a version token, and it is why this costs so much less than global coordination. On write the server returns the log position it assigned; the client stores it and sends it back on the next read. The replica serves the read if its applied position is at least the token, or waits, or forwards. That is a per-session constraint, not a global one: one integer, no cross-node round trips. Sticky routing achieves the same coarsely by pinning a session to a replica, and breaks on failover. All four guarantees together give causal consistency within a session, which is why they so often turn out to be the actual requirement.

L4.prompt_tpl: A user updates their profile, gets a success response, and the next page load shows the old value about {pct}% of the time. Name the violated guarantee, explain the mechanism producing it, and give two fixes with their failure modes.
L4.answer: Read-your-writes. The write went to the primary; the subsequent read was load-balanced to a lagging replica. Fix 1: sticky sessions pinning the user to one replica, which breaks on failover or rebalancing. Fix 2: return the write's version token and require the read to be served at or above that version, waiting or rerouting otherwise; costs a small latency tail when the chosen replica is behind.
L4.explanation: The percentage tracks replica count and lag: with one lagging replica out of two, roughly half of reads land on it. Fix 2 is strictly stronger because it survives routing changes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rank these by implementation cost for a {r}-replica deployment, cheapest first, and say what each one does not give you: sticky sessions, version tokens, monotonic reads via a per-client watermark, full causal consistency.
L4.answer: Sticky sessions (cheapest, gives nothing after failover or rebalance); monotonic reads via a client watermark (no read-your-writes across sessions or devices); version tokens (read-your-writes and monotonic reads, but no ordering between different clients); full causal consistency (orders across clients, but needs dependency metadata on every update and buffering on delivery).
L4.explanation: The ladder is the useful artefact: each rung adds one ordering guarantee and one piece of metadata. Most user-visible complaints are solved on the second or third rung.

The definition, in full:

  if no new updates are made to an object, eventually all reads return the last
  updated value.

Note the two quantifiers it omits: HOW LONG is eventually, and WHAT may be read
before then. Both are unbounded.

The useful replacement is a measured pair:
  p50 / p99 replication lag        e.g. 12 ms / 400 ms
  the anomaly set visible meanwhile e.g. stale reads, no monotonicity, lost updates
L0.cloze:
Eventual consistency says that if updates {{c1::stop}}, replicas {{c2::converge}}.
It bounds neither {{c3::how long}} nor {{c4::what anomalies are visible}} before then.
Replace it with a measured {{c5::lag distribution}} plus a named anomaly set.

concepts.L1: If updates stop, replicas converge. Says nothing about when, or what you read meanwhile.
concepts.L2: 'Eventual consistency' with no bound is nearly a non-guarantee. The useful question is always 'eventual within what bound, and what anomalies are visible before then'.
concepts.L3: Bailis and Kingsbury's Probabilistically Bounded Staleness work made this measurable rather than rhetorical: for a Dynamo-style store with $N$, $R$, $W$ and a measured write-propagation distribution, you can compute the probability that a read at $t$ milliseconds after a write returns the new value. On real hardware they found $N=3$, $R=W=1$ converged to 99.9 percent consistent reads within about 200 ms in one deployment, and much slower in another. That is the shape of an answer worth having. The reason 'eventual' alone is nearly vacuous is that a system that never converges until updates cease, and updates never cease, satisfies the definition while being permanently wrong.

L4.prompt_tpl: A store replicates with measured propagation p50 = {p50} ms and p99 = {p99} ms. A read is issued $t$ ms after a write to a different replica. Sketch how you would compute the probability of a stale read at $t$, and state the two facts eventual consistency alone gives you.
L4.answer: Model propagation delay as a distribution $F$; the probability of a stale read at time $t$ is approximately $1 - F(t)$ for a single replica, and for $R$ of $N$ reads you compose the per-replica probabilities. At $t = p50$ roughly half of reads are stale; at $t = p99$ roughly 1 percent are. Eventual consistency alone gives you neither number: only that the limit as $t$ grows is 0, and nothing about the path.
L4.explanation: This is the Probabilistically Bounded Staleness framing. The engineering answer is always a distribution plus an anomaly list, never the word eventually.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor's SLA says 'eventually consistent, typically under {ms} ms'. Write the three questions that turn this into a usable guarantee.
L4.answer: 1. What is the p99 and p99.9 of replication lag, measured how and under what load? 2. Which anomalies are visible before convergence: stale reads only, or also non-monotonic reads, lost updates, and read skew across keys? 3. What happens during a partition, since the convergence claim is conditioned on updates stopping and the network healing.
L4.explanation: Typically is a p50 claim dressed as a guarantee. The anomaly set matters more than the lag: stale-but-monotonic is usable, non-monotonic is not.

State-based (CvRDT). Give a type three things:

  1. a set of states $S$ with a partial order $\leq$
  2. a binary merge $\sqcup : S \times S \to S$ that is the LEAST UPPER BOUND
  3. an update function that is INFLATIONARY: $s \leq f(s)$

merge must be:  commutative   $a \sqcup b = b \sqcup a$
                associative   $(a \sqcup b) \sqcup c = a \sqcup (b \sqcup c)$
                idempotent    $a \sqcup a = a$

Those three laws are exactly what makes delivery order, duplication and retries
irrelevant, so an unreliable network cannot break convergence.
L0.cloze:
A state-based CRDT is a {{c1::join-semilattice}}: merge is the {{c2::least upper bound}} and updates are {{c3::inflationary}}.
Merge must be commutative, {{c4::associative}} and {{c5::idempotent}}, which is exactly why message reordering, duplication and retries are harmless.

concepts.L1: A replicated type whose replicas converge without coordination, because its merge is the least upper bound of a join-semilattice. Shapiro, Preguica, Baquero and Zawirski, 2011. Convergence is a theorem about algebra, not a protocol guarantee.
concepts.L2: The three merge laws map one-to-one onto the three things a network does to you: reordering needs commutativity, regrouping needs associativity, and duplication needs idempotence. If you find yourself designing a merge that is not idempotent, you have not designed a CRDT, you have designed something that breaks on retry.
concepts.L3: The convergence proof is short. States form a join-semilattice, so every pair has a least upper bound. Each replica's state only moves up the lattice: local updates are inflationary and merges are joins, both monotone. If every update eventually reaches every replica, each replica's state is an upper bound of the same set of updates, and since the least upper bound is unique, all replicas hold the same value. This is strong eventual consistency: replicas that have delivered the same updates hold equal state, with no rollback and no consensus. The operation-based variant trades merge idempotence for exactly-once causal delivery.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone proposes a counter CRDT whose state is a single integer and whose merge is $a + b$. Show it breaks with {n} replicas, and give the standard correct design.
L4.answer: Addition is not idempotent: merging a state with itself doubles it, so a redelivered or re-gossiped state inflates the count without bound. The correct design is a G-Counter, a vector of per-replica counts merged elementwise by max (which is idempotent), with the value being the sum of entries. Decrements need a PN-Counter, two G-Counters, increments minus decrements.
L4.explanation: Elementwise max is the canonical join. The trick throughout CRDT design is to find a representation whose merge is a max or a union rather than an accumulation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Prove that a G-Set (grow-only set, merge $=$ union) converges, then explain why the same argument fails for a set supporting removal, using {n} replicas.
L4.answer: Union is commutative, associative and idempotent, and insertion only adds elements, so it is inflationary; states form the powerset lattice ordered by inclusion, and union is its least upper bound. All replicas that have seen the same insertions hold the same set. Removal breaks inflation: deleting an element moves down the lattice, so merge (union) simply resurrects it, and the states no longer form a monotone sequence.
L4.explanation: This is why every removal-capable set CRDT encodes deletion as an addition to something else: tombstones in 2P-Set, or removed unique tags in OR-Set.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why an operation-based CRDT can drop the idempotence requirement on its operations, and what it must demand from the delivery layer instead, for {n} replicas.
L4.answer: Operation-based CRDTs require operations to commute but be applied exactly once, so the network layer must provide reliable causal broadcast with duplicate suppression. Idempotence is traded for exactly-once causal delivery. That is a heavier network requirement, which is why state-based designs dominate where the channel is unreliable and op-based ones dominate where a causal broadcast layer already exists.
L4.explanation: The two variants are inter-convertible, and the choice is really about where you want to pay: in state size and merge cost, or in delivery machinery.

L0.body:
Four sets, in order of how badly they behave.

  G-Set     add only. merge = union. correct, useless for deletion.
  2P-Set    two G-Sets: added A, removed R. value = A \ R.
            merge = union of both. Once removed, an element can NEVER be re-added.
  LWW-Set   timestamp every add and remove; last writer wins.
            Correct if clocks are trusted; silently drops writes if they are not.
  OR-Set    add(e) attaches a unique tag; remove(e) drops only tags the remover
            has SEEN. Concurrent add and remove: ADD WINS. Usually correct.
L0.cloze:
2P-Set stores added and removed sets; once removed an element can {{c1::never be re-added}}.
LWW-Set breaks when {{c2::clocks}} are untrusted.
OR-Set attaches a {{c3::unique tag}} per add and removes only {{c4::tags the remover has seen}}, so concurrent add and remove resolves {{c5::add-wins}}.

concepts.L1: The catalogue of set CRDTs and what each one silently gives up. All four converge; they differ in which concurrent-operation outcome they choose, and three of the four choose something a user will call a bug.
concepts.L2: Convergence is not correctness. Every design here converges by construction; the question is always what it converges to. LWW-Set with unsynchronised clocks converges to whichever replica had the faster clock, discarding real writes with no error, and that is the most common CRDT-shaped production incident.
concepts.L3: Work the OR-Set. Replica A adds $x$ with tag $t_1$; replica B concurrently adds $x$ with tag $t_2$, then removes $x$, which removes only $t_2$ since that is all B has seen. After merge the element set for $x$ is $\{t_1\}$, non-empty, so $x$ is present: add wins. Under 2P-Set the same history removes $x$ permanently, and under LWW-Set the outcome depends on two clocks that may differ by more than the operation gap. OR-Set costs metadata: tags accumulate, so real implementations compress them into version vectors rather than storing raw tags. Automerge and Yjs apply the same ideas to sequences, where the hard part becomes interleaving.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two replicas, initially empty. A: add(x); B: add(x); B: remove(x). After full merge, is x present under 2P-Set, LWW-Set and OR-Set? Assume B's clock is {skew} ms ahead of A's.
L4.answer: 2P-Set: absent, and permanently unaddable, since x is in the removed set forever. OR-Set: present, because B's remove only cancelled B's own tag and A's tag survives (add wins). LWW-Set: depends on the skew; with B's clock ahead, B's remove carries the later timestamp and x is absent even though A's add may have happened later in real time.
L4.explanation: The LWW answer changing with clock skew is the point: it converges to a value determined by clock error rather than by the operations, and it reports no conflict.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are building a shopping cart replicated across {r} regions with no coordination. Choose a CRDT for the item set and justify it against the alternatives, naming the anomaly each rejected option produces.
L4.answer: OR-Set, or a per-item PN-Counter for quantities. 2P-Set is disqualified because a user who removes an item can never re-add it. LWW-Set is disqualified because clock skew silently discards a genuine add. Add-wins is also the commercially correct bias: a resurrected item is a visible, correctable annoyance, whereas a silently dropped item is lost revenue.
L4.explanation: The Dynamo shopping-cart example makes the same argument informally. Choosing the bias deliberately, and choosing it toward the recoverable error, is the actual design decision.

  PHASE 1a  prepare(n)              to a majority of acceptors
  PHASE 1b  promise(n, accepted_n, accepted_v)   ignore anything numbered < n
  PHASE 2a  accept(n, v)   v MUST be the accepted_v carrying the highest
