  PHASE 2b  accepted(n, v)

Chosen when a majority sends accepted(n, v). Multi-Paxos keeps a stable leader
and skips phase 1 for later slots.
L0.cloze:
PHASE 1a {{c1::prepare(n)}} to a majority; acceptors promise to ignore proposals numbered {{c2::less than n}}.
In PHASE 2a the proposer must propose the value with the {{c3::highest accepted proposal number}} it heard, and may pick its own only if {{c4::none was returned}}.
Multi-Paxos skips {{c5::phase 1}} while the leader is stable.

concepts.L1: Prepare/promise then accept/accepted, with proposal numbers ensuring safety. Multi-Paxos amortizes the prepare phase with a stable leader.
concepts.L2: Single-decree Paxos is the elegant core; every practical system uses Multi-Paxos, and the gap between the paper and a working implementation is famously enormous. Lamport wrote a second paper because the first was considered incomprehensible.
concepts.L3: The whole safety argument lives in one line of phase 2a: a proposer may not propose its own value if any acceptor reports a previously accepted one. Suppose value $v$ was chosen with number $n$, meaning a majority accepted it. Any later proposer with number $m > n$ must gather promises from a majority, and any two majorities intersect, so at least one promise reports $(n, v)$ or something later. By the rule it must re-propose $v$. Induction over proposal numbers gives: once chosen, always chosen. Nothing else matters for safety, which is why the paper is short and every implementation is not: elections, log slots, reconfiguration, compaction and client sessions sit outside the proof.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Paxos implementation lets a proposer with number {n} propose its own value whenever fewer than half the promises carried an accepted value. Construct the two-proposer execution in which two different values are chosen.
L4.answer: Acceptors A,B,C. Proposer P1 with number 1 gets A and B to accept v1, so v1 is chosen. P2 with number 2 prepares and reaches B and C; only B reports (1, v1), which is one of two promises, fewer than half. Under the buggy rule P2 proposes v2, A and C accept, and v2 is chosen too. Two values chosen, agreement violated.
L4.explanation: The correct rule is unconditional: if any promise reports an accepted value, you must re-propose the one with the highest accepted number. Majority intersection guarantees you see the chosen value, but only one node may report it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why Multi-Paxos can skip phase 1 for slot {k} once a leader is stable, and precisely what event forces phase 1 to run again.
L4.answer: Phase 1 establishes a proposal number valid at a majority for all future slots, so a leader that already holds promises at number $n$ may issue accept messages directly for every subsequent slot. Phase 1 must rerun when a competing proposer prepares with a higher number, which revokes the promises, or when the leader restarts and cannot prove it still holds them.
L4.explanation: This amortisation is what makes Paxos one round trip in steady state, the same cost as Raft's AppendEntries. The two protocols are equivalent in the common path.

prereqs: Consensus and atomic broadcast are equivalent

The AppendEntries RPC, which is the whole protocol in one message.

  Arguments: term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit
  Results:   term, success

  Receiver:
   1. reply false if term < currentTerm
   2. reply false if log does not contain an entry at prevLogIndex
      whose term matches prevLogTerm            <-- the consistency check
   3. if an existing entry conflicts, delete it and everything after it
   4. append any new entries
   5. if leaderCommit > commitIndex:
          commitIndex = min(leaderCommit, index of last new entry)

AppendEntries carries {{c1::prevLogIndex}} and {{c2::prevLogTerm}}; the follower rejects unless its log matches there.
On conflict the follower {{c3::deletes the conflicting entry and all that follow}}.
commitIndex advances to {{c4::min(leaderCommit, index of last new entry)}}.

concepts.L1: Designed for understandability. Leader election with randomized timeouts, log replication with a strong leader, and the safety argument via the log matching and leader completeness properties.
concepts.L2: The joint consensus membership change protocol is the part most implementations get wrong or skip. Single-server changes are safer and simpler, and Ongaro's thesis (not the paper) covers this properly.
concepts.L3: The five safety properties are worth memorising as a checklist, because they are how you audit an implementation. Election safety: at most one leader per term, from one vote per server per term plus majority. Leader append-only: a leader never overwrites its own log. Log matching: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up to that index. Leader completeness: a committed entry is present in the log of every future leader, enforced by the up-to-date check in RequestVote. State machine safety: no two servers apply a different command at the same index. Everything else, elections, snapshots, membership, is machinery serving these five.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a {n}-node Raft cluster the leader crashes right after replicating an entry to one follower but before committing it. Enumerate the possible outcomes for that entry and say which Raft property decides each.
L4.answer: Either a future leader has the entry, in which case it may be committed later under the new term via the current-term commit rule, or a future leader lacks it, in which case it is silently overwritten. Which happens is decided by leader completeness plus the RequestVote up-to-date check: a candidate missing the entry can still win if a majority has logs no more up to date than its own. An uncommitted entry has no guarantee.
L4.explanation: This is why clients must not treat a replicated-but-uncommitted entry as durable, and why Raft's commit acknowledgement, not replication, is the client-visible boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rule 3 of AppendEntries deletes conflicting entries. Explain why deleting only the single conflicting entry at index {i}, rather than everything after it, breaks the log matching property.
L4.answer: Log matching says that if two logs agree at an index, they agree on everything before it, and the invariant is maintained by the leader only ever extending a prefix it has verified. If you delete one entry and keep later ones, the follower's log contains entries whose predecessors were never verified against the leader's, so two logs can share index and term at a later position while differing earlier. The induction that proves log matching collapses.
L4.explanation: Log matching is an inductive invariant maintained by the prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm check plus prefix truncation. Any partial truncation breaks the induction.

votedFor is {{c4::persisted}} so a restart cannot double-vote in one term.

concepts.L1: The election protocol and the two rules that make it safe: one persisted vote per term per server, and the log-comparison test that refuses to elect a server missing committed entries. Randomised timeouts handle liveness separately.
concepts.L2: The up-to-date comparison is by term first, index second, and reversing them is a real bug. A server with a longer log made of entries from a stale term is less up to date than a server with a shorter log ending in a newer term, because the longer log's tail was never committed and will be truncated.
concepts.L3: Why term dominates index: a term-5 leader may append many entries and crash before committing any, so they exist only on itself and a minority. Meanwhile a term-6 leader committed one entry to a majority. If index dominated, the term-5 server with the longer uncommitted tail could win, become leader and truncate a committed entry. Comparing terms first makes any holder of a term-6 entry outrank every log ending in term 5, whatever its length. For liveness: with a timeout drawn from $[T, 2T]$, the chance that two candidates fire within one broadcast interval falls geometrically per round, so $T$ an order of magnitude above broadcast time keeps expected elections near 1.

L4.prompt_tpl: Server A's log ends at index {ia} term 5. Server B's ends at index {ib} term 6. Which can win an election over the other, and what would happen if the up-to-date check compared index before term?
L4.answer: B can win: its lastLogTerm 6 beats A's 5, regardless of A's longer log. A cannot win against B. If index were compared first, A would win, become leader, and force B to truncate its term-6 entries, which may include committed ones. That violates leader completeness and can un-commit an acknowledged write.
L4.explanation: The longer log is the stale one here: A's extra entries are uncommitted term-5 leftovers. Term-first is what encodes that.

L4.prompt_tpl: An operator sets every node's election timeout to exactly {t} ms to make failover deterministic. Explain what breaks, and what property of the system is unaffected.
L4.answer: Split votes become likely to repeat: all followers time out together, all become candidates, each votes for itself, no one gets a majority, and the next round repeats the same synchronisation. Liveness degrades and can stall for many rounds. Safety is unaffected: one persisted vote per term still forbids two leaders in a term, so the cluster is merely slow to elect, never incorrect.
L4.explanation: This is the practical face of FLP: with deterministic timeouts a livelock is possible. Randomisation makes the rounds independent so failure probability decays geometrically.

L4.prompt_tpl: A follower receives RequestVote for term {t}, grants the vote, replies, and persists votedFor asynchronously. Describe the resulting safety violation.
L4.answer: If the follower crashes after replying and before the write reaches disk, it restarts with no record of the vote and can vote again in term t for a different candidate. Two candidates can then each assemble a majority in term t and both become leader, each committing different entries at the same index. Election safety and state-machine safety both fall.
L4.explanation: Raft's persistence requirement is explicit: currentTerm, votedFor and log entries must be durable before the RPC reply, not after. This is the single most commonly cut corner.

The optimisation returns {{c4::conflictTerm and conflictIndex}} so one round trip skips a whole term.

concepts.L1: Log matching says two logs agreeing at some index and term agree on the entire prefix. It is an inductive invariant, maintained solely by the AppendEntries consistency check plus prefix truncation, and it is what lets a leader repair any follower.
concepts.L2: The naive one-decrement-per-RPC repair is $O(\text{entries})$ round trips, which after a long partition means minutes of a follower stuck out of the quorum. The paper mentions the optimisation in a single paragraph and most tutorials skip it; without it a cluster that partitions for an hour takes an hour to converge.
concepts.L3: Proof, by induction on log growth. Base: empty logs agree. Step: a leader only appends to its own log, and a follower appends only after verifying its entry at prevLogIndex has term prevLogTerm. By the hypothesis, matching at an index implies matching on the prefix, so the follower's prefix now equals the leader's; truncation removes the divergent suffix. Combined with one leader per term and leaders never overwriting their own entries, this makes an entry uniquely identified by its (index, term) pair across the cluster.

L4.prompt_tpl: Leader log terms by index: 1,1,2,3,3. Follower log terms: 1,1,2,4,4,4. Using the naive decrementing repair, how many AppendEntries round trips are needed before the first success, and how many with the conflictTerm optimisation, for a divergence of {d} entries? Answer with the number of round trips the naive repair needs.
L4.answer: Naive: one round trip per rejected index. Here nextIndex starts at 6, and prevLogIndex values 5, 4, 3 are tried, so 3 failures then success, that is 4 round trips; in general $d+1$ for a divergence of $d$ entries, so 4, 11 and 101. With the conflictTerm optimisation the follower reports term 4 first appearing at index 4, so the leader jumps straight to prevLogIndex 3: 2 round trips regardless of $d$, one per divergent term.
L4.explanation: The optimisation turns a per-entry cost into a per-term cost. Divergences almost always span few terms and many entries, which is why it matters.

L4.prompt_tpl: State the log matching property and prove the induction step, given that at most {n} leader exists per term and a leader never overwrites its own log.
L4.answer: Property: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then the logs are identical in all entries up through that index. Step: a follower appends only after confirming its entry at prevLogIndex has term prevLogTerm, which by the hypothesis makes its prefix equal to the leader's; truncation removes any divergent suffix; therefore after the append the follower's log through the new entries equals the leader's. Uniqueness of the leader per term ensures no two distinct entries ever share an (index, term) pair.
L4.explanation: The two premises are load-bearing. Without one-leader-per-term, two different entries could share an (index, term) and the property is false at the base case.

  replicated on a majority. It commits such entries only INDIRECTLY, by
  committing an entry from its OWN current term at a higher index.

     AND log[N].term == currentTerm          <-- this conjunct is the rule

the leader can commit its predecessors' entries immediately.

A leader commits an entry only when a majority holds it AND {{c1::log[N].term == currentTerm}}.
Entries from previous terms are committed {{c2::indirectly}}, by committing a current-term entry above them.
The standard trick is to append a {{c3::no-op}} entry on election.

concepts.L1: Raft's commit rule has an extra conjunct beyond majority replication: the entry must be from the leader's current term. Without it, a replicated-on-a-majority entry can still be overwritten by a later leader.
concepts.L2: This is the single most commonly omitted line in Raft implementations, and the resulting bug is invisible until a specific five-node interleaving occurs. Counting replicas is intuitive and wrong; the counterexample is Figure 8 of the paper and it is worth being able to draw from memory.
concepts.L3: The counterexample, five servers S1 to S5. (a) S1 is leader in term 2 and replicates entry 2 to S2. (b) S1 crashes; S5 is elected in term 3 with votes from S3, S4 and itself, and appends its own entry at index 2. (c) S5 crashes; S1 returns, is elected in term 4, and replicates its term-2 entry at index 2 to S3, so it now sits on a majority (S1, S2, S3). If S1 committed it here on majority alone and then crashed, (d) S5 could be elected again in term 5 using votes from S2, S3, S4 (its last log term 3 beats their term 2) and overwrite index 2 with its own entry, destroying a committed entry. Requiring log[N].term == currentTerm blocks step (c), and the no-op makes the block cheap.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Raft implementation advances commitIndex whenever {m} of 5 nodes report matchIndex at or above N. Draw the five-server execution from the paper that loses a committed entry, and give the one-line fix.
L4.answer: The Figure 8 execution: S1 leader term 2 replicates index 2 to S2; crashes. S5 elected term 3 (votes S3, S4), appends its own index 2. Crashes. S1 elected term 4, replicates the old term-2 entry to S3 giving a majority, commits it, crashes. S5 elected term 5 (votes S2, S3, S4, since its last term 3 beats term 2) and overwrites index 2. Fix: require log[N].term == currentTerm before advancing commitIndex.
L4.explanation: Majority replication is necessary but not sufficient for commitment in Raft. Only a current-term entry's majority proves that no future leader can lack it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why appending a no-op entry immediately after winning an election in term {t} is not merely an optimisation but changes the observable availability of the cluster.
L4.answer: Without it, entries from previous terms stay uncommittable until some client happens to write, so a read-heavy cluster can hold acknowledged-looking-but-uncommitted entries indefinitely after a failover, and linearizable reads that depend on the commit index stall. The no-op creates a current-term entry at once, letting the leader commit its whole prefix and begin serving reads.
L4.explanation: This is why almost every production implementation appends a no-op on election. It converts an unbounded stall into one round trip.

    lastIncludedIndex   the index of the last entry in the snapshot
    lastIncludedTerm    its term      <-- needed for the AppendEntries check
    latest cluster configuration      <-- else membership is lost on restart

  InstallSnapshot(term, leaderId, lastIncludedIndex, lastIncludedTerm,

Sent when the leader has already discarded the entries a follower needs, i.e.
nextIndex[i] <= leader's lastIncludedIndex.

A snapshot must record {{c1::lastIncludedIndex}}, {{c2::lastIncludedTerm}} and the latest {{c3::cluster configuration}}.
lastIncludedTerm is needed so the {{c4::AppendEntries consistency check}} still works at the snapshot boundary.
InstallSnapshot is sent when the leader has {{c5::discarded}} the entries the follower needs.

concepts.L1: Log compaction by replacing a prefix with a state-machine snapshot. Servers snapshot independently, which is safe because the log prefix is already committed and applying it is deterministic, so every replica's snapshot at the same index is identical.
concepts.L2: The two fields people forget are lastIncludedTerm and the embedded configuration. Without the term, the consistency check has nothing to compare at the snapshot boundary; without the configuration, a server that restarts from a snapshot has no idea who is in the cluster and can vote in an election it should not.
concepts.L3: Why independent snapshotting is safe, and why InstallSnapshot exists anyway. Snapshots cover only committed entries, which are identical on all servers by log matching, so no coordination is needed. The problem is bandwidth: a far-behind follower needs entries the leader has discarded, so the leader ships bytes. Implementation notes: snapshotting must not block the state machine (copy-on-write or fork); the snapshot must be fsynced before the log prefix is truncated, or a crash loses both; and a follower must discard a snapshot whose lastIncludedIndex is below its own commitIndex rather than regress. The last one, missed, causes silent state rollback.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Raft state machine holds {mb} MB and receives 5000 entries per second at 200 bytes each. Snapshots are taken every {n} entries. Give the steady-state log size between snapshots and the per-snapshot write volume, then say which cost dominates. Answer with the per-snapshot write volume in MB.
L4.answer: Log growth is 5000 times 200 = 1 MB/s. Between snapshots the log holds n times 200 bytes: 2 MB at n=10000, 20 MB at n=100000. Each snapshot writes the full state, mb MB. At mb=500 and n=10000 you write 500 MB every 2 seconds, 250 MB/s, versus 1 MB/s of log: the snapshot dominates by 250 times. Raising n to 100000 gives 500 MB every 20 seconds, 25 MB/s. Snapshot cost dominates unless the interval is large or the snapshot is incremental.
L4.explanation: The lesson is that snapshot frequency, not log growth, sets your write amplification. This is why production systems use incremental or copy-on-write snapshots keyed to state size rather than entry count.

L4.prompt_tpl: A follower at commitIndex {ci} receives InstallSnapshot with lastIncludedIndex {li} and replaces its state machine with the snapshot. Explain the resulting anomaly and the guard that prevents it.
L4.answer: The snapshot is older than the follower's committed state, so replacing the state machine rolls it backwards: committed entries between li and ci are lost, and a client that read them can now read older values. The guard is to ignore any snapshot whose lastIncludedIndex is at or below the receiver's own lastApplied or commitIndex, keeping only the log suffix.
L4.explanation: State rollback on a stale snapshot is silent and violates state-machine safety. The guard is one comparison and is routinely missing.

Two protocols. Use the second unless you need the first.

  JOINT CONSENSUS (paper). Pass through $C_{old,new}$, where every decision
  needs a majority of BOTH configurations:
     $C_{old}$ -> $C_{old,new}$ (committed) -> $C_{new}$
  A server adopts a config entry when it APPENDS it, not when it commits it.

  SINGLE-SERVER CHANGE (thesis). Add or remove ONE server at a time: any two
  configurations differing by one server have overlapping majorities, so no
  joint phase is needed. One uncommitted change at a time; a joiner catches
  up as a non-voting learner first.

Under joint consensus, decisions in $C_{old,new}$ need a majority of {{c1::both}} configurations.
A server uses a configuration entry as soon as it {{c2::appends}} it, not when it commits it.
Single-server changes work because configurations differing by {{c3::one}} server have {{c4::overlapping majorities}}.
A joining server should first run as a non-voting {{c5::learner}}.

concepts.L1: Changing the set of servers without stopping the cluster. The danger is a window in which the old and new configurations can each independently elect a leader, which is exactly what both protocols are built to exclude.
concepts.L2: The rule that a server obeys a configuration entry on append rather than on commit is counterintuitive and mandatory. If servers waited for commit, an entry could be committed under a configuration some servers do not yet know, producing two disjoint majorities.
concepts.L3: Why one at a time is safe: go from $C = \{a,b,c\}$ (majority 2) to $C' = \{a,b,c,d\}$ (majority 3). Any 2-subset of $C$ and any 3-subset of $C'$ must intersect, since $2 + 3 = 5 > 4$. So no leader can be elected in $C$ and another in $C'$ at the same time. The same holds for removal. Now go from 3 to 5 in one step: majorities 2 and 3 over a 5-set need $2 + 3 = 5 > 5$, which is false, so $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c,d,e\}$ can elect two leaders simultaneously. That is precisely the bug joint consensus exists to prevent. Ongaro's thesis also documents the removed-leader case: a leader not in $C_{new}$ must step down only after committing $C_{new}$, and must not count itself.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show whether a direct one-shot change from a {a}-node to a {b}-node configuration can produce two leaders, by comparing majority sizes and the total membership.
L4.answer: Old majority is floor(a/2)+1, new majority floor(b/2)+1, over a union of at most b servers when the old set is a subset. Two disjoint majorities exist iff old_majority + new_majority is at most b. For 3 to 5: 2 + 3 = 5, not greater than 5, so disjoint majorities exist and two leaders are possible. For 4 to 7: 3 + 4 = 7, again not greater than 7, so possible. For 3 to 7: 2 + 4 = 6, at most 7, possible. Any jump of more than one server is unsafe.
L4.explanation: The safety condition is that every old majority intersects every new majority. Adding or removing one server at a time is exactly the largest step that always satisfies it.

L4.prompt_tpl: An implementation applies a configuration entry only once it is committed, adding {k} servers one at a time. Construct the execution in which two leaders coexist.
L4.answer: Leader L in C_old appends C_new (adding d) and replicates it to a minority, then partitions away. Servers that appended but did not commit C_new still act under C_old. L, still using C_old, can commit the entry using an old-configuration majority while the servers holding C_new elect their own leader under the new-configuration majority. Two leaders, two configurations, no overlap enforced.
L4.explanation: Adopting the configuration on append closes the window: any server that has even seen C_new counts votes under it, so the two configurations can never be simultaneously live in disjoint majorities.

In roughly descending frequency.

  1. currentTerm / votedFor / log not fsynced before the RPC reply
  2. commitIndex advanced on majority alone, no log[N].term == currentTerm check
  3. truncating the log on a reordered AppendEntries rather than a real conflict
  4. a stale leader serving local reads with no lease, no quorum round trip

  6. no client session table: a retried command executes twice

Bug 2: advancing commitIndex without the {{c2::current-term}} conjunct.
Bug 3: truncating the follower log on a {{c3::reordered}} AppendEntries rather than a real conflict.
Bug 4: a stale leader serving reads with no {{c4::lease or quorum round trip}}.
Bug 6: no {{c5::client session table}}, so a retried command executes twice.

concepts.L1: The defect catalogue that separates a Raft implementation that passes tests from one that survives a Jepsen run. Every item is a place where the paper is explicit and the code usually is not.
concepts.L2: Bug 3 is the subtlest: AppendEntries is not idempotent under reordering unless you truncate only on an actual term conflict. A delayed RPC carrying fewer entries can otherwise delete entries the follower has correctly received, and the resulting data loss looks like a network problem.
concepts.L3: Trace bug 4, the stale-leader read, since it is the one that ships. Leader L is partitioned from the cluster but does not know it. The majority elects L' and commits new writes. L still believes it is leader, its own state machine is intact, and it answers a read locally. The client gets a value that is arbitrarily stale, and the system is not linearizable despite consensus being correct throughout. Two fixes exist. ReadIndex: confirm leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority before answering, one round trip per read batch. Or a leader lease shorter than the minimum election timeout, answering locally, trading a clock assumption for latency.

L4.prompt_tpl: Review a Raft-backed configuration store that serves reads from whichever node the client connects to, for {n} nodes. List the failure modes in severity order and give the two standard fixes with the assumption each requires.
L4.answer: Worst: any follower may be arbitrarily behind, so reads are not even monotonic across a reconnect. Next: a partitioned stale leader answers with pre-partition state indefinitely. Fixes: ReadIndex, where the leader records commitIndex, confirms leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority, then serves once applied, requiring no clock assumption but costing a round trip; or a leader lease shorter than the minimum election timeout, serving locally, requiring bounded clock drift.
L4.explanation: Consensus on writes does not give you consistent reads. Read path design is a separate decision with its own assumptions, and it is where most Raft-based systems lose linearizability.

L4.prompt_tpl: A follower receives two AppendEntries RPCs out of order: first one carrying entries up to index {hi}, then a delayed one carrying entries only up to index {lo}. The implementation truncates the log to the length of each incoming request. What is lost, and what is the correct rule?
L4.answer: The delayed RPC truncates entries between lo and hi that the follower had correctly stored, and if the leader had already counted them toward a commit the cluster can lose a committed entry. The correct rule is to truncate only when an existing entry actually conflicts, that is has the same index but a different term, and otherwise to keep the longer suffix and append only genuinely new entries.
L4.explanation: The paper's rule 3 says 'if an existing entry conflicts with a new one'. Truncate-to-length is a paraphrase that is wrong under reordering, and networks reorder.

concepts.L2: Sloppy quorums break the overlap guarantee entirely — Dynamo-style systems with sloppy quorums are not quorum systems in the safety sense. This is stated in the Dynamo paper and widely ignored.

That common node holds the latest write, so the read sees it. Sloppy quorums break the premise, not the arithmetic: the $W$ nodes are chosen from whoever is reachable, so the write set may lie entirely outside the $N$ nodes the reader will consult. Dynamo's paper is explicit about this and about hinted handoff being a best-effort repair. Any system advertising tunable consistency with sloppy quorums enabled is advertising a probability, not a guarantee.

L4.explanation: The tradeoff is symmetric: every node you subtract from R you must add to W. Majority-majority is the unique choice that maximises the minimum of the two availabilities.

L4.answer: With N=6, R=W=3 the sum is 6, which is not strictly greater than 6, so two quorums can be disjoint and a read can miss a committed write. With N=4, R=W=2 the sum is 4, same problem. L4.explanation: Even N buys no extra fault tolerance over N-1 and makes the strict inequality easy to violate. That is the practical reason for odd cluster sizes.

Each step gives roughly a 30-fold reduction on a base that is already 30 times smaller, so absolute savings collapse while quorum size and write latency grow monotonically.
L4.explanation: Beyond five, the availability gain is smaller than the noise from correlated failures, while the write path waits on one more replica. That is why five is the near-universal choice.

L0.body:
A lease is a lock with an expiry that the HOLDER cannot extend unilaterally.
A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued with it.

  1. client A acquires lease, gets token 33
  2. A stalls: GC pause / page fault / VM migration, 40 s
  3. lease expires; client B acquires it, gets token 34
  4. B writes to storage with token 34; storage records 34
  5. A wakes up, still believes it holds the lease, writes with token 33
  6. storage REJECTS: 33 < 34

Without step 6 the lease is a suggestion. Redlock has no token, which is
Kleppmann's objection to it.
L0.cloze:
A lease is a lock with an {{c1::expiry}}; the holder cannot extend it unilaterally.
The token must be {{c2::monotonically increasing}} and checked by the {{c3::storage layer}}, which rejects any token lower than one it has already seen.
Redlock is unsafe for correctness because it produces no {{c4::fencing token}}.

concepts.L1: Two mechanisms that together make distributed mutual exclusion safe. The lease bounds how long a holder may believe it holds the lock; the fencing token lets the resource itself reject a writer whose belief is stale.
concepts.L2: The lease alone is never sufficient, because a process can be paused for longer than any lease you choose: a stop-the-world GC, a hypervisor migration, or an fsync stall on a degraded disk. Only the resource can adjudicate, and it can do so only if writes carry an ordering token it checks.
concepts.L3: The reason a lease is safer than a lock is asymmetric trust. A lock's holder decides when to release; a lease's grantor decides when it ends, so the grantor can safely assume expiry without hearing from anyone. That converts a crashed holder wedging the system into a bounded wait. But expiry is judged on the grantor's clock while the holder acts on its own, and those diverge by an unbounded pause. Hence the token: it moves the final check to the only party that observes the real order of writes. Raft leader leases are the same construction, with the lease shorter than the minimum election timeout so a stale leader's local reads cannot outlive its successor's election.

L4.prompt_tpl: A job scheduler grants a {sec}-second lease and workers check `if lease_valid(): write_output()`. Occasionally two workers' outputs interleave in one file. Explain the exact interleaving and give the fix.
L4.answer: Worker A checks the lease, passes, then is descheduled by a GC pause longer than the lease. The lease expires, worker B acquires it and writes. A resumes and writes with a valid-looking but expired belief. The check-then-act gap is unbounded because the pause is unbounded. Fix: issue a monotonic fencing token with the lease and have the output store reject any write whose token is below the highest it has seen.
L4.explanation: No lease duration fixes this, since the pause has no bound. The fix must live in the resource, not the client.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare a Raft leader lease of {ms} ms against ReadIndex for serving linearizable reads. State the assumption each requires and the failure mode of each.
L4.answer: Lease: serve locally while the lease holds, requiring the lease to be shorter than the minimum election timeout and bounded clock drift between leader and followers. Failure mode is a clock jump or a long pause letting a stale leader answer after a new one is elected. ReadIndex: confirm leadership by a heartbeat round to a majority before answering, requiring no clock assumption but costing one round trip per read batch. Failure mode is added latency, not incorrectness.
L4.explanation: The choice is a clock assumption against a round trip. ReadIndex batching amortises the round trip across concurrent reads, which usually makes it the better default.

L0.body:
Nodes in a total order: writes at the head, reads at the tail.

  write: client -> [HEAD] -> [node] -> [TAIL] -> ack to client
  read:  client ---------------------------> [TAIL] -> reply

Invariant: each node's history is a PREFIX of its predecessor's, so anything
readable at the tail is already on every node.

Failures: head -> successor takes over, in-flight writes lost; tail ->
predecessor takes over; middle -> splice out, predecessor resends its suffix.

CRAQ: keep multiple versions and read at ANY node; if the local copy is dirty,
ask the tail for the committed version number.
L0.cloze:
Writes enter at the {{c1::head}} and are acknowledged by the {{c2::tail}}; reads are served at the {{c3::tail}}.
Each node's history is a {{c4::prefix}} of its predecessor's.
{{c5::CRAQ}} lets any node serve reads by asking the tail for the committed version when its own copy is dirty.

concepts.L1: Nodes in a chain, writes at the head propagating to the tail, reads at the tail. Strong consistency with better throughput than primary-backup, since the read load sits on a different node from the write load.
concepts.L2: CRAQ extends it to allow reads at any node with version checking. Underappreciated design, used in production by several storage systems, and mentioning it in a design discussion is a real differentiator.
concepts.L3: Why the prefix invariant gives linearizability for free. A write is acknowledged only when it reaches the tail, and it reaches the tail only after every node, so at acknowledgement time all nodes hold it. Reads at the tail therefore never see a value that is not fully replicated, and never miss one that was acknowledged. No quorum, no version comparison, no consensus round: correctness comes from the topology. The throughput argument: a quorum makes every node do both read and write work, while a chain puts write work on $n-1$ nodes and read work on the tail alone. The cost is write latency, linear in chain length, and a dependency on a separate consensus service for reconfiguration.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}-node chain has 1 ms per hop. Compare write latency and read latency against a majority-quorum system of the same size with 1 ms round trips, and state which workload favours which. Answer with the chain write latency in milliseconds, counting the direct reply.
L4.answer: Chain write latency is n-1 propagation hops (2, 4, 6 ms for n = 3, 5, 7) plus the ack path: roughly 2(n-1) ms if the ack returns along the chain, or n-1 plus one direct reply from the tail, giving n ms total: 3, 5, 7 ms for n = 3, 5, 7. Chain reads are one hop to the tail, about 1 ms, and never contend with writes. Quorum writes and reads are both about 1 ms (one round trip to the majority), but every node serves both. Chains favour read-heavy workloads; quorums favour low write latency and larger clusters.
L4.explanation: The crossover is set by the read-to-write ratio and by n, since chain write latency grows linearly with chain length while quorum latency does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your storage layer is {r} percent reads and needs strong consistency. Argue for chain replication with CRAQ over a Raft-based design, and name the dependency it introduces.
L4.answer: CRAQ serves reads at any of n nodes, so read throughput scales linearly with chain length while Raft concentrates linearizable reads on the leader or pays a ReadIndex round trip. At 90 to 99 percent reads that is the dominant factor. The dependency introduced is an external configuration service (ZooKeeper or similar) to detect failures and reconfigure the chain, since the chain cannot agree on its own membership.
L4.explanation: The honest tradeoff: chain replication moves consensus out of the data path and into a separate control plane. You still need consensus, you just need less of it per request.

L0.body:
PBFT's three phases, normal-case operation with $n = 3f+1$ replicas.

  client -> primary:      REQUEST
  primary -> all:         PRE-PREPARE(view, seq, digest)
  all -> all:             PREPARE(view, seq, digest, i)
      wait for $2f$ matching PREPAREs   -> 'prepared': order fixed within the view
  all -> all:             COMMIT(view, seq, digest, i)
      wait for $2f+1$ matching COMMITs  -> 'committed-local': order fixed ACROSS views
  all -> client:          REPLY
  client waits for $f+1$ matching replies.

Cost: $O(n^{2})$ messages per request, versus $O(n)$ for Raft.
L0.cloze:
PBFT uses $n = $ {{c1::3f+1}} replicas and three phases: pre-prepare, {{c2::prepare}}, commit.
Prepare fixes the order {{c3::within a view}}; commit fixes it {{c4::across views}}.
The client accepts an answer after {{c5::f+1}} matching replies.
Message cost is $O(n^{2})$ per request.

concepts.L1: PBFT and successors tolerate arbitrary (malicious) failures with 3f+1 nodes for f faults. Much more expensive than crash-fault-tolerant consensus.
concepts.L2: Almost never the right choice inside a trust boundary. Its relevance is blockchain and cross-organizational systems. Knowing when not to reach for it is more useful than knowing the protocol.
concepts.L3: The two-phase structure exists for a reason worth knowing. Prepare establishes that $2f+1$ replicas agree on a sequence number for this request in this view; that is enough to prevent two requests getting the same number while the view lasts. But a view change can elect a primary that never saw those prepares. Commit closes the gap: once $2f+1$ replicas have committed, any new-view construction must include an honest replica holding the commit certificate. Applied to real decisions: inside one company, BFT defends against an attacker who already has code execution on a minority of replicas, and does nothing about the correlated bug in the binary all of them run.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare message counts for one request at $f = {f}$: Raft with $2f+1$ nodes versus PBFT with $3f+1$. Give both totals and the ratio. Answer with the PBFT message total.
L4.answer: Raft: the leader sends AppendEntries to $2f$ followers and receives $2f$ replies, about $4f$ messages. PBFT: pre-prepare is $3f$ messages, prepare is $3f$ senders times $3f$ recipients roughly $(3f+1)3f$, commit the same, plus $3f+1$ replies. For f=1: Raft 4, PBFT about 3 + 12 + 12 + 4 = 31, ratio roughly 8. For f=2: Raft 8, PBFT about 6 + 42 + 42 + 7 = 97, ratio 12. For f=3: Raft 12, PBFT about 9 + 90 + 90 + 10 = 199, ratio 17.
L4.explanation: The ratio grows with $f$ because PBFT's two all-to-all phases are quadratic while Raft is linear. This, plus 50 percent more machines, is the real cost of the Byzantine model.

L4.prompt_tpl: For each, say whether BFT is warranted and why: (a) a {n}-node etcd cluster inside one VPC, (b) a settlement network run jointly by {n} competing banks, (c) a fleet of edge devices in customer premises reporting telemetry.
L4.answer: (a) No: one trust boundary, correlated binary bugs dominate, and BFT does not detect them. (b) Yes: no single party is trusted, participants have financial incentive to equivocate, and the trust boundary runs between organisations. (c) Partly: devices are outside your control so their inputs are untrusted, but the answer is input validation and attestation, not BFT consensus among devices.
L4.explanation: The rule is that BFT is warranted when the trust boundary runs between the replicas. If all replicas are yours, you have an integrity problem, not a consensus problem.

L0.body:
Two clocks, two purposes. Confusing them is a bug class.

  clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)   wall clock. NTP steps it. It can go BACKWARDS.
  clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)  since boot. Never steps. Not comparable
                                  across machines.

  measuring a duration     -> MONOTONIC, always
  timestamping an event    -> REALTIME, and never compare across machines

Typical NTP accuracy: 1-50 ms in a datacenter, worse over WAN. Observed skew
across a cluster is routinely tens of milliseconds; PTP gets to microseconds
with hardware support.
L0.cloze:
Use {{c1::CLOCK_MONOTONIC}} for durations because it never {{c2::steps backwards}}.
CLOCK_REALTIME can jump backwards when {{c3::NTP}} corrects it.
Cluster clock skew is routinely {{c4::tens of milliseconds}}, so wall-clock comparison across machines is never a valid {{c5::ordering}}.

concepts.L1: NTP gives millisecond-ish accuracy with jumps and drift. Clock skew across a cluster is routinely tens of milliseconds. Never use wall-clock comparison for ordering across machines.
concepts.L2: Leap seconds have caused real production outages. Google smears them across the day rather than stepping; understanding why is a good concrete example of clock reasoning.
concepts.L3: The leap-second case makes the failure concrete. On 30 June 2012 the inserted leap second caused Linux kernels to livelock in a hrtimer path; Reddit, Mozilla and others went down, and the fix at many sites was to restart every machine. The kernel bug was real, but the deeper issue is that a repeated second breaks any code assuming time strictly increases. Google's answer is the leap smear: spread the extra second over 24 hours by running clocks about 0.0012 percent slow, so no second repeats and no jump occurs. The cost is that a smeared clock disagrees with UTC by up to 500 ms mid-smear, which is fine unless you compare across a smear boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: A job computes elapsed = time() - start using the wall clock, and NTP steps the clock back {ms} ms mid-run. Give the computed elapsed value's sign, the downstream effect on a {sec}-second timeout, and the fix.
L4.answer: Elapsed can be negative, or simply too small by the step. A timeout comparison then never fires, so the operation hangs for up to the timeout plus the step, and in a retry loop it may never fire at all. The fix is CLOCK_MONOTONIC for every duration measurement; the wall clock is only for timestamps a human or another machine will read.
L4.explanation: The rule is one line: never subtract two wall-clock readings. Every language has a monotonic source and most default to the wrong one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two servers each timestamp an event with their wall clocks, {ms} ms apart in real time, with measured NTP offsets of up to 40 ms each. Can you order the events from the timestamps? State the condition under which you can.
L4.answer: Only if the timestamp difference exceeds the sum of the uncertainty bounds, here 80 ms. At 10 ms apart the order is undecidable from timestamps. At 100 ms apart it is decidable, since 100 > 80. This is exactly the reasoning TrueTime formalises by returning an interval rather than a point.
L4.explanation: The general rule: a wall-clock comparison is meaningful only when the gap exceeds the combined uncertainty. Systems that ignore this silently produce wrong orderings.

L0.body:
Three rules, one integer per process.

  local event:      $C_i \mathrel{+}= 1$
  send(m):          $C_i \mathrel{+}= 1$;  attach $C_i$ to $m$
  receive(m):       $C_i = \max(C_i, C_m) + 1$

Total order: break ties by process id, giving $(C_i, i)$ lexicographically.

Guarantee:      $a \to b \implies C(a) < C(b)$
NOT guaranteed: $C(a) < C(b) \implies a \to b$
L0.cloze:
On receive, $C_i = $ {{c1::\max(C_i, C_m) + 1}}.
Ties are broken by {{c2::process id}} to get a total order.
The implication runs one way only: $a \to b$ implies {{c3::C(a) < C(b)}}, but the converse is {{c4::false}}.

concepts.L1: A counter per process, incremented on events, max'd on receive. Gives a total order consistent with causality, but the order is arbitrary among concurrent events.
concepts.L2: Lamport timestamps can order events that are actually concurrent, so a < b does not imply a caused b. The one-way implication is the whole subtlety and it's frequently stated backwards.
concepts.L3: Run it and the one-way implication becomes obvious. $P_1$ does three local events: $C = 1, 2, 3$. $P_2$, never having communicated, does one: $C = 1$. Now compare $P_1$'s second event ($C=2$) with $P_2$'s ($C=1$). The timestamps say $P_2$'s came first, but no message ever passed between them: the events are concurrent, and the ordering is an artefact of counting. This is exactly the failure when engineers use a Lamport clock to decide which of two conflicting writes to keep: it will pick one deterministically, which looks like conflict resolution and is actually a silent lost update. To detect concurrency rather than manufacture an order, you need a vector.

L4.prompt_tpl: $P_1$ and $P_2$ both start at $C = 0$. $P_1$: event a, event b, send(m) to $P_2$. $P_2$: event c, event d, receive(m), event e. Give the Lamport timestamp of every event and identify which pairs the timestamps order but which are actually concurrent, with {n} processes.
L4.answer: $P_1$: a=1, b=2, send=3. $P_2$: c=1, d=2, receive = max(2,3)+1 = 4, e=5. Timestamps order c(1) before b(2), and d(2) equal to b(2) broken by id, yet a, b and the send are concurrent with c and d: no message links them. Genuinely ordered: send(3) before receive(4), and everything before them in program order.
L4.explanation: The receive jumps to 4, not 3, because the rule adds one after the max. Skipping that increment breaks the strict inequality when a send and a receive would otherwise tie.

L4.prompt_tpl: A key-value store resolves conflicting writes by keeping the one with the higher Lamport timestamp, tie-broken by node id, across {n} nodes. Describe the data loss and the correct alternative.
L4.answer: Two genuinely concurrent writes get different Lamport timestamps purely from local event counts, so the store silently discards one with no conflict reported. A busy node's writes systematically win over a quiet node's. The correct alternative is a version vector, which reports the pair as concurrent so the application can merge, or a CRDT whose merge is defined for concurrent updates.
L4.explanation: Lamport timestamps are for producing a total order when any order will do. They are the wrong tool for detecting conflicts, because they cannot represent concurrency.

L0.body:
One counter per process, carried on every message.

  local event at $i$:   $V_i[i] \mathrel{+}= 1$
  send from $i$:        $V_i[i] \mathrel{+}= 1$; attach $V_i$
  receive at $i$:       $V_i[k] = \max(V_i[k], V_m[k])$ for all $k$; then $V_i[i] \mathrel{+}= 1$

Comparison:
  $V_a \leq V_b$   iff $V_a[k] \leq V_b[k]$ for every $k$
  $a \to b$        iff $V_a \leq V_b$ and $V_a \neq V_b$
  $a \parallel b$  iff neither $V_a \leq V_b$ nor $V_b \leq V_a$

Size: $O(n)$ integers per message with $n$ processes.
L0.cloze:
On receive, take the elementwise {{c1::max}} then increment {{c2::your own}} entry.
$a \to b$ iff $V_a \leq V_b$ elementwise and they are {{c3::not equal}}.
If neither dominates, the events are {{c4::concurrent}}.
The cost is {{c5::O(n)}} per message.

concepts.L1: A vector of counters, one per process. Captures causality exactly — you can detect concurrency, not just order.
concepts.L2: Cost is O(n) per message with n nodes, which is why they don't scale to large or dynamic clusters. Dotted version vectors and version vectors with pruning are the practical mitigations.
concepts.L3: The comparison is a partial order on vectors, and that is exactly why vector clocks capture causality where Lamport timestamps cannot: the vector order has incomparable pairs, and a single integer's order does not. Two events with $V_a = (2,0,1)$ and $V_b = (1,3,0)$ are incomparable, so they are concurrent, and the system can report a conflict instead of inventing a winner. The $O(n)$ cost is per message and per stored version, so a 100-node cluster carries 100 integers with every value, and departed nodes leave entries no one can safely drop. Version vectors and dotted version vectors are the practical answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: Three processes. $P_1$: local, local, send to $P_2$. $P_2$: local, receive, send to $P_3$. $P_3$: local, receive. Give every vector and state whether $P_3$'s first local event is concurrent with $P_1$'s first, for {n} processes.
L4.answer: $P_1$: (1,0,0), (2,0,0), send (3,0,0). $P_2$: (0,1,0); receive gives max then increment: (3,2,0); send: (3,3,0). $P_3$: (0,0,1); receive: (3,3,2). $P_3$'s first local event (0,0,1) versus $P_1$'s first (1,0,0): neither dominates, so they are concurrent, which is correct since no message chain connects them.
L4.explanation: The receive rule is max-then-increment-own. Doing the increment before the max, or omitting it, makes a send and its receive compare as equal.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cluster of {n} nodes stores a vector clock with each of {v} values, using 8-byte counters. Compute the metadata overhead in bytes per value and in total, and say at what cluster size this becomes the dominant cost for 200-byte values. Answer with the metadata overhead in bytes per value.
L4.answer: Overhead per value is 8n bytes: 80 B at n=10, 800 B at n=100, 8000 B at n=1000. For a million values that is 80 MB, 800 MB and 8 GB. Against a 200-byte value, metadata exceeds payload once 8n > 200, that is n > 25. So beyond about 25 nodes the clock costs more than the data.
L4.explanation: This is why Dynamo-style systems use version vectors keyed by replica (a handful of entries) rather than per-client vector clocks, and why they cap and truncate the list.

concepts.t: Version vectors and dotted version vectors

L0.body:
Three things called vector clocks that are not the same object.

  vector clock    one entry per PROCESS; causality between events
  version vector  one entry per REPLICA; bounded by replica count
  DVV             a version vector plus a DOT: the (replica, counter) pair
                  identifying this write itself

Why the dot: two clients read context A:2 and write concurrently. Plain version
vectors give the second a larger vector, so it seems to supersede the first,
which is dropped. With dots they are (A,3) and (A,4), both with context A:2:
neither dominates, so both survive.
L0.cloze:
A {{c1::version vector}} has one entry per replica; a vector clock has one per process.
A dotted version vector adds a {{c2::dot}}, the (replica, counter) pair identifying the write itself.
Without the dot, two concurrent writes on the same context get {{c3::identical}} vectors and one is {{c4::silently lost}}.

concepts.L1: Three distinct data structures that share a name. The distinction that matters operationally is per-replica versus per-client entries, and the dot, which lets a single replica represent two concurrent writes from different clients without losing one.
concepts.L2: Sibling explosion is the real-world failure, not the theory. Under plain version vectors a Riak or Dynamo key written by many concurrent clients accumulates unbounded siblings or silently drops writes, depending on which bug you have. DVVs bound sibling count by the number of concurrent clients, not by total writes.
concepts.L3: Work the losing case. Replica A holds version $\{A:2\}$. Client 1 reads it, and so does client 2. Client 1 writes back with context $\{A:2\}$: A increments to $\{A:3\}$. Client 2 writes back with the same context $\{A:2\}$: A increments to $\{A:4\}$, and since $\{A:3\} \leq \{A:4\}$, A concludes the second write causally supersedes the first and discards it. But the two clients never saw each other's write, so they were concurrent and both should survive. The dot fixes this by tagging each write with the exact counter it consumed: write 1 is $(A,3)$ with context $\{A:2\}$, write 2 is $(A,4)$ with context $\{A:2\}$, and neither context dominates the other's dot, so both are kept as siblings.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two clients read the same version of a key, counter {k} at replica A, and write back concurrently. Under plain version vectors, how many versions survive, and how many under DVV? Explain the discrepancy.
L4.answer: Plain version vectors: 1 survives, because the second write produces a strictly larger vector that appears to dominate the first. DVV: 2 survive as siblings, because each write carries its own dot and neither client's causal context includes the other's dot. The discrepancy is that a plain vector cannot distinguish 'later at this replica' from 'causally after'.
L4.explanation: The single-replica case is where plain version vectors quietly fail. The dot restores the distinction between replica-local sequencing and causality.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}-replica store is accumulating thousands of siblings per hot key. Diagnose the two possible causes and give the fix for each.
L4.answer: Cause 1: clients writing without supplying the causal context they read, so every write is concurrent with every other and nothing can ever be pruned. Fix: require read-before-write and pass the context token. Cause 2: plain version vectors with per-client entries growing without bound. Fix: switch to dotted version vectors keyed by replica, which bound siblings by concurrent client count rather than total writes.
L4.explanation: Sibling count is a diagnostic: it should track concurrency, not traffic. Growth proportional to write volume means the causal context is being dropped somewhere.

HLC state per node: $(l, c)$, a physical-time component and a counter.

  send or local event at $j$:
      $l' = l_j$;  $l_j = \max(l', pt_j)$
      if $l_j = l'$ then $c_j \mathrel{+}= 1$ else $c_j = 0$

  receive $(l_m, c_m)$:
      $l' = l_j$;  $l_j = \max(l', l_m, pt_j)$
      if   $l_j = l' = l_m$  then $c_j = \max(c_j, c_m) + 1$
      elif $l_j = l'$        then $c_j \mathrel{+}= 1$
      elif $l_j = l_m$       then $c_j = c_m + 1$
      else                        $c_j = 0$

Guarantee: $a \to b \implies (l_a, c_a) < (l_b, c_b)$, with $l_j$ within the clock
skew of real time.
L0.cloze:
HLC keeps a pair $(l, c)$: $l$ tracks {{c1::physical time}} and $c$ is a {{c2::logical counter}}.
It guarantees $a \to b$ implies $(l_a, c_a) <$ {{c3::(l_b, c_b)}}, like a Lamport clock.
Unlike a Lamport clock, $l$ stays within the {{c4::clock skew}} of real time, so timestamps remain human-meaningful.

concepts.L1: Combine physical time with a logical counter. Timestamps are close to physical time and still respect causality. Used in CockroachDB and MongoDB.
concepts.L2: The practical sweet spot — you get human-meaningful timestamps that are also causally correct, without needing atomic clocks.
concepts.L3: HLC is a Lamport clock whose physical component is dragged forward by the wall clock. Both properties fall out of that. Causality holds because the pair is compared lexicographically and every send or receive strictly increases it, exactly as in a Lamport clock. Bounded drift holds because $l_j$ only advances to the max of local physical time and any received $l$, and every node's physical time is within the NTP bound, so $l$ cannot run ahead by more. The counter absorbs events sharing a millisecond. The payoff over TrueTime is no special hardware and no commit-wait; the cost is causal consistency and consistent snapshots rather than external consistency.

L4.prompt_tpl: Node A has HLC $(100, {ca})$ and physical time 100. It receives a message stamped $(100, {cm})$. Give A's new HLC. Then give it for the case where A's physical time has advanced to 105.
L4.answer: Case 1: $l' = 100$, $l_A = \max(100, 100, 100) = 100$, and since $l_A = l' = l_m$, $c_A = \max(c_A, c_m) + 1$. For (3,7) that is 8; for (0,2) that is 3. Case 2 with $pt = 105$: $l_A = \max(100, 100, 105) = 105$, which equals neither $l'$ nor $l_m$, so $c_A = 0$, giving $(105, 0)$.
L4.explanation: The counter resets whenever physical time makes real progress, which is what keeps it small. It only grows while many events share the same physical millisecond.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need consistent snapshots across {n} shards and cannot buy atomic clocks. Argue for HLC over both Lamport clocks and TrueTime, and state precisely what you give up relative to Spanner.
L4.answer: Over Lamport clocks: HLC timestamps are close to physical time, so a snapshot at timestamp T means roughly wall-clock T, and clients can request snapshots by real time. Over TrueTime: no GPS or atomic clocks and no commit-wait, so writes have no artificial latency floor. What you give up is external consistency: two causally unrelated transactions can be ordered against real time, since HLC bounds drift but does not wait it out.
L4.explanation: This is the CockroachDB position exactly: HLC plus an uncertainty interval that triggers a read restart, giving serializability without the hardware or the commit-wait.

  $\epsilon$ = half the interval width: a sawtooth of about 1 to 7 ms over the
  30-second poll against GPS and atomic-clock masters.

  Commit:  $s$ = TT.now().latest
           ... Paxos ...
           wait until TT.after($s$)     // commit-wait, expected $2\epsilon$
           release locks
L0.cloze:
TT.now() returns an {{c1::interval}} guaranteed to contain the true time; its half-width $\epsilon$ is about {{c2::1 to 7}} ms.
The commit protocol picks $s = $ TT.now().{{c3::latest}}, then waits until TT.{{c4::after}}(s) before releasing locks.
That wait, about {{c5::2 epsilon}}, is the mechanism, not an overhead to optimise away.

concepts.L1: Spanner's approach: GPS and atomic clocks give a bounded uncertainty interval, and transactions wait out the uncertainty before committing. Buys external consistency at the cost of ~7ms commit wait.
concepts.L2: The insight is that you can buy semantics with hardware. Spanner deliberately waits — commit-wait is not an optimization to remove, it's the mechanism. That inversion surprises people.
concepts.L3: Follow what commit-wait buys. If transaction $T_1$ commits at timestamp $s_1$ and only releases its locks once $s_1$ is definitely in the past everywhere, then any transaction $T_2$ that starts afterwards must pick $s_2 > s_1$, because $T_2$'s TT.now().latest is at least the true time, which now exceeds $s_1$. So timestamp order agrees with real-time order: external consistency, which is strict serializability. Delete the wait and the guarantee goes, since $T_2$ on a machine whose clock reads low could pick $s_2 < s_1$. The implication is that the guarantee costs latency proportional to clock uncertainty, so better clocks make the database faster.

L4.prompt_tpl: TrueTime reports $\epsilon = {eps}$ ms. Give the expected commit-wait, and the availability consequence if a machine's local clock drifts far enough that $\epsilon$ grows to {bad} ms. Answer with the expected commit-wait in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Commit-wait is about $2\epsilon$: 2, 8 and 14 ms. At $\epsilon = 50$ ms every read-write transaction waits about 100 ms, and at 200 ms about 400 ms, so write throughput on any serially dependent key collapses to roughly $1/(2\epsilon)$, that is 10 or 2.5 per second. Spanner's response is to evict a machine whose uncertainty exceeds a threshold rather than let it slow the system.
L4.explanation: This inverts the usual relationship: in Spanner, clock quality is a performance parameter, and a bad clock is an availability incident rather than a correctness one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why Spanner does not simply skip commit-wait and compare timestamps directly, given that $\epsilon$ is only about {eps} ms and typical inter-transaction gaps are larger.
L4.answer: Because correctness cannot rest on a typical gap. Two transactions separated by less than $2\epsilon$ would be ordered by whichever machine's clock happened to read higher, so a transaction that really came second could get a smaller timestamp, and a snapshot read at that timestamp would see the later write but not the earlier. The wait converts a probabilistic ordering into a guaranteed one.
L4.explanation: The commit-wait is the mechanism, not an implementation cost. Removing it does not make Spanner faster and slightly weaker; it makes Spanner not strictly serializable.

L0.body:
The marker rule, for FIFO channels. No process halts.

  initiator: record own state; send MARKER on every outgoing channel
  on MARKER from channel $c$:
      FIRST marker seen:  record own state; record $c$ as EMPTY;
                          send MARKER on all outgoing channels;
                          start recording all other incoming channels
      otherwise:          stop recording $c$; what you recorded is $c$'s state

Result: a CONSISTENT CUT. No recorded receive lacks its send. It need not be a
state the system was ever in. Flink's checkpoint barriers are this algorithm.
L0.cloze:
The snapshot algorithm sends a {{c1::marker}} on every outgoing channel and records the channel state as the messages arriving {{c2::between the first marker and that channel's marker}}.
The result is a {{c3::consistent cut}}: no recorded receive is missing its send.
The snapshot need not be a state the system was {{c4::ever actually in}}.
Flink's {{c5::checkpoint barriers}} are the same construction.

concepts.L1: A global snapshot taken without stopping the system. Markers flow along channels; each process records its own state on first seeing a marker, and records each channel's in-flight messages as those arriving before that channel's marker.
concepts.L2: The snapshot is a consistent cut, not a moment in time. The recorded state may never have existed simultaneously, yet any stable property true in it was true in the run. Enough for deadlock detection, GC and recovery; not enough for auditing what the state was at 14:00.
concepts.L3: Why a consistent cut is what recovery needs. Restoring from it, every message recorded as in flight is replayed, and every recorded process state already reflects the sends that produced those messages. So the restored system is a legal continuation of the original run: no message is delivered twice and none is lost. Flink turns this into exactly-once processing: barriers are injected at the sources, each operator buffers the inputs whose barrier arrived until all inputs deliver it, then snapshots and forwards. Alignment makes the cut consistent and also makes checkpointing stall under backpressure, which is why unaligned checkpoints exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: A distributed snapshot of {n} processes reports a state in which process 1 has sent a message that process 2 has not received, and the message is not in any recorded channel. Is the snapshot correct? What went wrong?
L4.answer: It is incorrect: a consistent cut may contain a send without a receive (the message is in flight and must appear in a channel state), but never a receive without a send, and never a send whose message vanishes. A message that is neither delivered nor recorded means channel recording stopped too early, typically because the process stopped recording that channel before its marker arrived, or because the channel is not FIFO.
L4.explanation: The algorithm's correctness rests on FIFO channels. On a non-FIFO channel a marker can overtake data messages and the cut loses them, which is why implementations sequence-number the channel.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Flink job's checkpoints start taking {min} minutes and eventually time out under load. Explain the mechanism through barrier alignment and give two fixes with their tradeoffs.
L4.answer: Under backpressure a slow input delivers its barrier late, and every operator with multiple inputs buffers the fast inputs until it arrives, so alignment time grows with the skew and the checkpoint stalls. Fix 1: unaligned checkpoints, which snapshot in-flight buffers instead of waiting, at the cost of larger checkpoint size and slower recovery. Fix 2: remove the backpressure, by fixing the slow operator or rebalancing partitions, which is the real fix.
L4.explanation: Alignment cost is proportional to input skew, so checkpoint duration is a backpressure symptom. Treating it as a checkpoint-tuning problem addresses the alarm rather than the fire.

Phi-accrual: output a suspicion level, not a boolean.

  keep a sliding window of the last $n$ heartbeat inter-arrival times
  fit a distribution (normal, or exponential for tail-heavy networks)
  let $t$ = time since the last heartbeat

      $$\phi(t) = -\log_{10}\big(1 - F(t)\big)$$

  where $F$ is the fitted CDF. $\phi = 1$ means about 10 percent chance of a
  false positive if you declare death now; $\phi = 2$ about 1 percent;
  $\phi = 3$ about 0.1 percent.

Cassandra defaults to a threshold of 8. Akka defaults to 10.
L0.cloze:
Phi-accrual outputs a {{c1::suspicion level}} rather than a boolean.
$$\phi(t) = -\log_{10}(1 - F(t))$$
$\phi = 2$ corresponds to about a {{c2::1 percent}} false-positive rate.
The window {{c3::adapts}} to observed network variance, so a slow network raises the bar automatically.

concepts.L1: Perfect detection is impossible asynchronously. Phi-accrual detectors output a suspicion level rather than a binary, adapting to observed network variance.
concepts.L2: Fixed timeouts are the wrong abstraction and cause both false positives during GC pauses and slow detection during real failures. Phi-accrual (used in Cassandra and Akka) is the practical answer.
concepts.L3: Why a fixed timeout is the wrong shape. A fixed threshold encodes one hypothesis about the network and is wrong in both directions: during a stop-the-world GC pause of 800 ms a 500 ms timeout declares a healthy node dead, and on a genuinely dead node a conservatively-set 30 s timeout leaves the cluster degraded for half a minute. Phi-accrual replaces the threshold with a distribution fitted to what this network actually does, so the same $\phi$ threshold means the same false-positive probability whether inter-arrival times have a 5 ms or a 200 ms standard deviation. The threshold now has units of confidence rather than milliseconds, which is a decision an operator can reason about.

L4.prompt_tpl: Heartbeat inter-arrivals have mean {mu} ms and standard deviation {sd} ms, roughly normal. Compute the delay after the last heartbeat at which $\phi$ reaches 2, and state what false-positive rate that threshold encodes. Answer with the delay in milliseconds at which phi reaches 2.
L4.answer: $\phi = 2$ means $1 - F(t) = 10^{-2}$, so $t$ is the 99th percentile of the fitted distribution: $t = \mu + 2.326\sigma$. For mu=100, sd=20: 146.5 ms. For mu=100, sd=50: 216.3 ms. For mu=500, sd=20: 546.5 ms. For mu=500, sd=50: 616.3 ms. The threshold encodes a 1 percent chance of wrongly declaring a live node dead at that instant.
L4.explanation: The key property is that the same phi gives the same false-positive rate under any variance, so a noisier network automatically waits longer without any operator retuning.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your JVM service pauses for up to {gc} ms in old-generation GC. Compare a fixed {to} ms timeout against phi-accrual with threshold 8, and say what each does during the pause and during a real crash.
L4.answer: Fixed timeout: fires during every long GC pause, causing spurious failovers and, in a leader-based system, an election and lost throughput. Phi-accrual with threshold 8 corresponds to roughly a 1-in-100-million false-positive rate, so it tolerates the pause if pauses are represented in the fitted window, and still detects a real crash within a few missed heartbeats because phi rises without bound as silence continues.
L4.explanation: Phi-accrual does not eliminate false positives; it makes their rate an explicit, tunable parameter instead of an emergent property of one hard-coded number.

L0.body:
The network does not partition into clean halves. It does this:

  A <-> B   ok
  B <-> C   ok
  A <-> C   BROKEN        <- a partial partition. Not symmetric, not transitive.

With a leader-based protocol:
  - A and C alternate winning elections forever; B votes for whoever asks
  - a node can be the leader's follower and unreachable from half the cluster
  - failure detectors on A and C disagree permanently

One-way partitions exist too: A can send to B while B cannot send to A.
A heartbeat that tests one direction will never notice.
L0.cloze:
In a {{c1::partial}} partition, A-B and B-C work while A-C does not; connectivity is not {{c2::transitive}}.
Leader-based protocols can enter perpetual {{c3::election churn}}, because a third node votes for either side.
A {{c4::one-way}} partition defeats any heartbeat that tests only one direction.

concepts.L1: Real network failures are rarely a clean split. Links fail individually and asymmetrically, so connectivity is neither symmetric nor transitive, and protocols that assume a partition divides the cluster into two consistent groups behave in ways their proofs never covered.
concepts.L2: The dangerous case is not lost availability but perpetual leader churn: a node that can reach a majority but not the current leader will keep starting elections, winning, being displaced, and repeating, so the cluster is technically live and practically useless. Raft's PreVote and CheckQuorum extensions exist for exactly this.
concepts.L3: Trace the churn. Five nodes; node C can reach A, B and D but not the leader E, while everyone else reaches E fine. C's timer fires, it increments its term and requests votes. A, B and D see a higher term, step down and vote for C. E, told of the higher term, steps down, but E is still reachable by A, B and D, so when its own timer fires it wins term $n+2$ and C starts over. Throughput goes to zero while every safety property holds. PreVote fixes it by making a candidate confirm it could win before incrementing its term; CheckQuorum makes a leader step down when it cannot reach a majority. Jepsen generates exactly these topologies because they break systems that survive clean partitions.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}-node Raft cluster shows a leader change every few seconds with no node down and no packet loss on most links. One node cannot reach the leader. Explain the cycle and name the two mitigations.
L4.answer: The isolated-from-leader node times out, increments its term, and requests votes; the others see the higher term, step down, and elect it. The old leader, still reachable by the majority, then times out and wins the next term, and the cycle repeats. Mitigations: PreVote, where a candidate must win a straw poll before incrementing its term, and CheckQuorum, where a leader steps down if it cannot reach a majority.
L4.explanation: The cluster never violates safety, and every node reports itself healthy. This is why leader-change rate is a first-class metric: it detects a class of failure that liveness checks miss.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design a health check that detects a one-way partition between {n} nodes. State what a naive check misses and what the correct check reports.
L4.answer: A naive check has A ping B and read the reply, which passes if A-to-B works and fails only if the return path also fails, so it cannot distinguish direction. The correct check is a bidirectional gossip in which each node publishes its own view of who it can reach, and the cluster compares views: a link that A reports as up and B reports as down is a one-way failure. Report the asymmetry, not a boolean.
L4.explanation: Reachability is a directed graph and must be measured as one. Systems that store a single symmetric up/down bit per peer cannot represent the failure they are hunting.

The observability gap that defines it:

  the system's own health check:   SUCCESS   (200 OK, 5 ms, from localhost)
  the client's experience:          3 percent errors, p99 at 8 s

Shapes:
  a disk returning correct data at 1/50th the usual throughput
  a NIC dropping 2 percent of packets, which TCP hides as latency
  one of 64 shards hot, so the mean still looks fine
  a node accepting connections but never completing TLS handshakes

Huang et al. 2017 call this DIFFERENTIAL OBSERVABILITY: the system's own
failure detector and its clients disagree about its health.

Gray failure is defined by {{c1::differential observability}}: the system and its clients disagree about its health.
Health checks pass because they test {{c2::the wrong thing from the wrong place}}.
Failover does not trigger, so the degraded component stays {{c3::in the serving set}}.

concepts.L1: A component that is degraded but not dead — slow, or failing a subset of requests. Far more damaging than clean crashes because failover doesn't trigger.
concepts.L2: Most severe production incidents are gray failures, and most fault tolerance design assumes fail-stop. This gap is where the real operational pain lives, and naming it is a mature-engineer signal.
concepts.L3: The fix is architectural, not a better threshold. Health checks must be issued by the party that experiences the failure, over the path that matters, and must measure the distribution rather than the mean. Three moves. Percentiles: measure p99 and p99.9, since a component fine for 97 percent of requests is invisible in a mean. Graded detection: a degraded node gets less traffic rather than being kept or evicted wholesale, which is phi-accrual applied to load balancing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service's own dashboards are green while {pct} percent of client requests fail. The health check is an HTTP GET to /healthz on localhost. List three specific gray failures this check cannot see and the replacement check for each.
L4.answer: 1. A NIC dropping packets: localhost bypasses the network entirely, so check from a peer over the real path. 2. L4.explanation: A health check that shares no code path with a real request is testing the process's ability to answer health checks. That is almost always what a green dashboard during an outage means.

L4.prompt_tpl: One node in a {n}-node fleet is serving correct responses at one twentieth normal throughput. Argue whether to evict it, and describe the load-balancing policy that handles it without a binary decision.
L4.answer: Evicting is correct here, but a binary policy is fragile because the same mechanism will evict healthy nodes during a load spike. The better policy is weighted load balancing on observed per-target latency and error rate, so a node at one twentieth throughput naturally receives about one twentieth the traffic, with a floor of probe traffic so it can recover and a cap on how much of the fleet may be down-weighted at once.
L4.explanation: Graded response is the general answer to gray failure: the failure is continuous, so the response should be too, with a global guard so the policy cannot evict the whole fleet.

concepts.t: RPC semantics and the exactly-once lie

L0.body:
Three deliverable semantics, and the one that is not.

  at-most-once   send once, never retry. Lost request -> lost operation.
  at-least-once  retry until acked. Duplicate execution is possible.
  exactly-once   NOT ACHIEVABLE over a lossy channel (two generals).

  exactly-once EFFECTS = at-least-once delivery
                       + idempotent handler or a persistent dedup record

The ambiguous case, which is the whole problem:

  client -> server: charge(100)
  server: charges, writes to db, sends response
  <response lost>
  client: timeout. Was it charged? THE CLIENT CANNOT TELL.
L0.cloze:
at-most-once retries {{c1::never}}; at-least-once retries until acked and may {{c2::execute twice}}.
Exactly-once {{c3::delivery}} is impossible over a lossy channel; exactly-once {{c4::effects}} are achievable with at-least-once delivery plus {{c5::idempotence or a dedup record}}.
On a timeout the client cannot distinguish a lost request from a lost response.

concepts.L1: The three semantics a remote call can offer, and the precise sense in which the third is marketing. What is achievable is exactly-once effects, built from at-least-once delivery plus a receiver that can recognise a repeat.
concepts.L2: The consequential asymmetry is that a timeout is not a failure. It is an unknown outcome, and code that treats it as failure will double-charge on retry while code that treats it as success will silently lose work. The only correct handling is to make the retry safe, then retry.
concepts.L3: Where the boundary sits determines the design. If the operation is naturally idempotent (PUT a full object, set a value, DELETE by id) the retry is free. If it is not (increment, append, charge, send email) you need a natural key (an order id, a message offset) or a supplied one, and the dedup record must be written in the same atomic unit as the effect. Written separately, the problem returns one layer down: the effect commits, the record does not, the retry re-executes. Kafka binds the producer-id sequence number and the output writes into one transaction; a database writes the key into a unique index in the same transaction as the charge.

L4.prompt_tpl: Classify each as naturally idempotent or not, and give the minimum machinery for a safe retry: (a) PUT /user/{uid} with a full body, (b) POST /account/deposit with amount {amt}, (c) DELETE /session/abc, (d) an email send.
L4.answer: (a) Idempotent: repeated PUT of the same body yields the same state, no machinery needed beyond last-write-wins semantics. (b) Not idempotent: needs a client-supplied idempotency key stored uniquely in the same transaction as the balance update. (c) Idempotent: deleting an absent session is a no-op, return 204 either way. (d) Not idempotent and not transactional with your database: use a dedup table keyed on a message id, accept that a crash between send and record can still duplicate, and make the email itself tolerant of duplication.
L4.explanation: Item (d) is the honest one: when the effect leaves your transactional boundary, exactly-once effects are unachievable and the right move is to make duplicates harmless.

L4.prompt_tpl: A handler charges a card, then inserts the idempotency key into a separate table, then returns. Under {n} retries after a crash between the two writes, what happens, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: The charge commits and the key does not, so the retry sees no key and charges again, once per retry. The fix is to write the key and the effect in one atomic unit: a single transaction containing both, with a unique constraint on the key, so a duplicate insert fails and the handler returns the stored response instead of re-charging.
L4.explanation: The dedup record must be atomic with the effect. Any ordering of two separate commits has a crash window that reintroduces duplication.
