L0.body:
Four papers, rising in operational usefulness and falling in fame.

  2007 Dynamo    consistent hashing, vector clocks, sloppy quorums, hinted
                 handoff, Merkle anti-entropy. The 2012 retrospective admits
                 it was hard to operate.
  2017 Aurora    'the log is the database': ship redo records, not pages;
                 quorum of 6 across 3 AZs, W=4, R=3
  2020 Physalia  millions of tiny Paxos cells for EBS lock management,
                 placed by topology to reduce correlated failure

Physalia is the best paper on blast radius as a design input.
L0.cloze:
Dynamo introduced consistent hashing, {{c1::vector clocks}}, sloppy quorums and Merkle-tree anti-entropy.
Aurora's central idea is that {{c2::the log is the database}}: ship redo records, not pages.
{{c3::Physalia}} places millions of tiny Paxos cells by {{c4::network topology}} to minimise correlated failure.

concepts.L1: Dynamo, then the Dynamo retrospective. Aurora. Physalia. The Millions of Tiny Databases paper.
concepts.L2: Physalia and the Aurora papers are more operationally interesting than Dynamo and much less read. Aurora's 'the log is the database' insight is a genuinely deep architectural idea.
concepts.L3: Aurora's insight repays study because it is a pure I/O-amplification argument. A traditional replicated database ships pages plus log plus double-write buffer to every replica, measured in the paper at roughly 7.4 times write amplification. Aurora ships only redo records to a storage fleet that materialises pages itself, and uses 6 replicas across 3 AZs with $W=4$, $R=3$, tolerating the loss of a whole AZ plus one node. Physalia's contribution is different: blast radius as a first-class placement constraint.

L4.prompt_tpl: Aurora uses $N = 6$ across 3 availability zones with $W = 4$ and $R = 3$. Verify the quorum inequalities, and determine whether it survives losing one full AZ plus {k} additional node.
L4.answer: $R + W = 7 > 6$, so read-write overlap holds. $W = 4 > 6/2 = 3$, so write-write overlap holds. Losing one AZ removes 2 nodes, leaving 4: writes still possible (exactly 4) and reads fine. Losing an AZ plus 1 more leaves 3: reads still work ($R=3$) but writes cannot reach 4, so the volume is read-only. Losing an AZ plus 2 leaves 2, below R, so neither works.
L4.explanation: The design target is stated in the paper as AZ+1 durability with continued read availability, which the arithmetic confirms exactly: 6/4/3 is the smallest configuration achieving it across 3 AZs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Dynamo's 2012 retrospective is unusually candid. Name {k} design decisions it identifies as operationally costly, and what Amazon's later systems did instead.
L4.answer: 1. Client-side conflict resolution via vector clocks pushed merge logic into every application, so later systems either use CRDTs with defined merges or avoid concurrent writes entirely. 2. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff gave availability but no real quorum guarantee, so DynamoDB moved to a leader-based, strongly-consistent-by-default design. 3. Operating a peer-to-peer ring at scale needed deep expertise, which is why DynamoDB became a managed service with a control plane rather than a library.
L4.explanation: The retrospective's honesty is the reason to read it: the paper that defined a decade of NoSQL design also documents which of its ideas did not survive contact with operations.

L0.body:
The core is the Dataflow model. Four questions, in order:

  WHAT   is computed?              transformations
  WHERE  in EVENT time?            windowing
  WHEN   in PROCESSING time?       watermarks and triggers
  HOW    do refinements relate?    accumulation mode

  event time      when the thing happened
  processing time when your system saw it
  watermark       a claim no event earlier than $t$ will arrive.
                  A HEURISTIC. Late data still happens.

Read: Kafka (2011), MillWheel (2013), Dataflow (2015), Naiad (2013), then
Flink's Lightweight Asynchronous Snapshots (2015).
L0.cloze:
The Dataflow model asks what, {{c1::where in event time}}, when in processing time, and how refinements relate.
A {{c2::watermark}} claims no further events earlier than $t$ will arrive, and it is a {{c3::heuristic}}.
Flink's checkpointing is {{c4::Chandy-Lamport}} applied to stream processing.

concepts.L1: Kafka, the Dataflow model, MillWheel, Naiad, Flink's checkpointing (Chandy-Lamport applied).
concepts.L2: The Dataflow paper's separation of event time from processing time, with watermarks and triggers, is the correct conceptual frame for all stream processing and it's genuinely clarifying.
concepts.L3: The event-time versus processing-time split is the whole insight, and it is best stated as a failure mode. Window by processing time and your results depend on when your system happened to receive data, so a lag spike silently changes your numbers and a replay disagrees with the original run. Window by event time and the result is a deterministic function of the data, reproducible across replays, at the cost of a watermark to decide when a window may close. The watermark is a heuristic, so the model makes lateness explicit: triggers decide when to emit, accumulation mode decides how a late emission relates to earlier ones, and allowed lateness bounds state retention.

L4.prompt_tpl: A pipeline windows by processing time in {min}-minute buckets. A consumer lag spike delays a batch by {delay} minutes. Describe exactly what happens to the output, and what changes if the pipeline windows by event time.
L4.answer: Events that occurred in one interval land in a later processing-time bucket, so one window under-counts and a later one over-counts. Re-running the pipeline produces different buckets again, because the assignment depends on receive time. With event-time windowing each event lands in the window its own timestamp selects regardless of arrival, so the result is deterministic; the lag instead delays the watermark, which delays window closure and may push some events past allowed lateness.
L4.explanation: Processing time makes your output a function of your infrastructure's behaviour. Event time makes it a function of the data, which is the only version that is reproducible.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your watermark is heuristic and about {pct} percent of events arrive after it. Give the three knobs the Dataflow model provides and what each costs.
L4.answer: 1. Allowed lateness: keep window state longer so late events are still incorporated, at the cost of state size and memory. 2. Triggers: emit an early speculative result and refine as more data arrives, at the cost of downstream consumers needing to handle updates. 3. Accumulation mode: accumulating (restate the whole window) or discarding (emit only the delta), which trades downstream simplicity against message size. Alongside these, feed dropped-late-data to a side output so the loss is measured rather than silent.
L4.explanation: The model's contribution is making all three explicit and independent. Systems that hard-code any of them force a single correctness-versus-latency tradeoff on every pipeline.

What to read for ideas that have not yet become folklore.

  FoundationDB  deterministic simulation testing: the whole cluster,
                single-threaded, virtual clock, seeded PRNG, faults as inputs
  Delta Lake    ACID over object storage from an ordered transaction log
                plus optimistic concurrency
  TAO           a read-optimised graph store whose cache tier IS the system
  Gorilla       in-memory time series, delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR
                float compression, about 12x smaller
  Scuba         in-memory sampled analytics for debugging
L0.cloze:
FoundationDB's contribution is {{c1::deterministic simulation testing}}: the whole cluster single-threaded with a virtual clock and a seeded PRNG.
{{c2::Delta Lake}} gets ACID over object storage from an ordered transaction log plus optimistic concurrency.
{{c3::Gorilla}} compresses time series with delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-encoded floats.

concepts.L1: FoundationDB's deterministic simulation testing. Delta Lake. TAO. Facebook's Scuba and Gorilla.
concepts.L2: FoundationDB's simulation testing approach — a deterministic single-threaded simulation of the entire cluster including failures — is arguably the most important testing idea in distributed systems, and it's barely known outside the field.
concepts.L3: Take the FoundationDB claim seriously and ask why it is not universal. The technique requires that every source of non-determinism (time, network, disk, thread scheduling, randomness) be injectable, which is an architectural constraint you must adopt before writing the storage layer. FoundationDB did, and could replay any failure from its seed, run years of simulated cluster time per week of wall clock, and inject faults at every step. Retrofitting means routing every I/O and timer through an interface, which is a rewrite. That is why the idea is admired more than copied, and why testing strategy is an architectural decision.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your team is starting a new storage system and can adopt one of these ideas as an architectural commitment. Pick one, justify it against the other {k}, and state its cost.
L4.answer: Deterministic simulation. It is the only one that must be decided before the first line of the storage layer, since retrofitting injectable time, network, disk and scheduling is a rewrite; the others (a transaction log over object storage, a cache-as-system tier, delta-of-delta compression) can be added later. Its cost is that every I/O and timer goes through an interface, which adds indirection, constrains library choice, and forbids ambient concurrency.
L4.explanation: The deciding question is reversibility. Commit up front only to the decisions you cannot make later, and simulation testing is the clearest example in this list.

L4.prompt_tpl: Delta Lake gets ACID over object storage, which offers no multi-object atomicity. Explain the mechanism, and what it requires from the object store for {n} concurrent writers.
L4.answer: An ordered transaction log: each commit writes a new numbered log file, and the version number is the serialization point. Writers read the current version, prepare data files, then attempt to write log entry N+1; only one can succeed. That requires the object store to provide atomic put-if-absent, or an external coordinator supplying it, since a store with last-writer-wins semantics would let two writers both believe they committed version N+1.
L4.explanation: This is the whole pattern behind lakehouse formats: object storage gives you durable immutable files, and a single-object atomic operation on the log turns them into a transactional table.
